title: Tuesday Miami Dolphins Thoughts With The Earl
summary: You know, I understand that this season is about growth, development, and resetting the outlook.  But is it too much to ask to get one game of complimentary football from this team?  Yet another frustrating loss when one side of the ball shows up, but the other does not.  Here’s what I saw. THE DEFENSE […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FL - NOVEMBER 08: Miami Dolphins running back Kaytron Allen (30) holds on to the ball despite as effort by Detroit Lions linebacker Joe Bachie (35) to punch it free during the game between the Detroit Lions and the Miami Dolphins on Sunday, November 8, 2026 at Hard Rock Stadium in Mami, FL (Photo by Icon Sportswire) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images You know, I understand that this season is about growth, development, and resetting the outlook. But is it too much to ask to get one game of complimentary football from this team? Yet another frustrating loss when one side of the ball shows up, but the other does not. Here’s what I saw. THE DEFENSE SHOWED UP I can really call them, can’t I? The Detroit Lions and Miami Dolphins had two of the league’s worst defenses coming into this game. I figured there would be a shootout, or at least a higher-scoring affair. Yet the game featured fewer than 500 total yards of offense and only 28 total points. The Lions averaged 29 PPG coming into this contest, scoring less than 20 points only once, and that was against the league’s best defense, the Vikings. They averaged 6 yards per play before this game. Yet, the Miami Dolphins defense limited the Lions to 19 points and 4.6 yards per play. The Lions gained over 100 fewer yards than their per-game average for the season. For the 1st time all season, the pass defense allowed less than a 70% completion percentage. Goff was limited to 6.8 YPA, and he did not throw a TD. He was sacked 3 times. Rookie Chris Johnson got an INT. Not only that, but the run defense showed up again. The Lions gained 102 yards, but 25% of it came on 2 misdirection plays. Jahmyr Gibbs has been the league’s most dominant weapon thus far this season, and he eventually found the end zone. But he was limited to 74 yards on 20 carries and no catches on 1 target. That’s a 3.7 YPC average, and that’s WITH 2 runs of 10+ yards. This was a terrible matchup for the Dolphins, but they stepped up in a big way. MALIK WILLIS IS HURT The offense picked a bad time to be absent. The Lions had allowed 300+ yards in every game but one so far, and that was to the offensively challenged Vikings. They were fairly decent in run defense, although I suspected that was due to lack of volume. They score so much that teams abandon the run. The Dolphins had 21 rushing attempts, which is a little below their standard. Gordon ran fairly well when he got an opening. However, the story is that Willis had 2 scrambles for 7 yards. The stat itself isn’t as striking as watching them happen. Willis is a dynamic runner, and we have seen him make big plays with his legs this season. But in the past 2 games, he has been reluctant to run. He has been on the injury report the past few weeks with a groin injury, but was listed as a full participant. It was obvious that the injury, or maybe something else, is hampering him. He ran slowly and lumbering, not at all like what we have seen from him. That doesn’t excuse the INT, which was a bad decision. But it can explain why he can’t escape pressure like he normally does, and why he ran the way I would have out there. I know fans hate excuses, but anyone who has ever dealt with a groin injury understands. You may feel fine walking around. But the moment you have to run and put forth effort, it’s very painful, and you can’t do it. It can affect everything, including throwing mechanics. Even with that, Willis had good moments. I don’t want to make this about whether he is good enough, but as long as he is limited, the offense will be limited. I honestly wouldn’t mind if they sat him for a while until he is healthy. In the past 2 games, he played at a higher level, and I believe that if he were 100% on Sunday, the Dolphins could have won. Well… there were other issues too. THIS AND THAT Dirty laundry as far as the eye could see. Officiating in the league has been bad this season and too often, the guy sin stripes have been too visible. This game was no exception as there were a combined 20 accepted penalties. This isn’t a “blame the refs” post though. The Dolphins were just bad in this regard. There was a huge pass play to Kevin Coleman Jr. that came back due to a holding penalty. Several drives had crushing penalties that put the offense way behind the sticks. This team doesn’t have the talent to overcome problems like excessive penalties. To invoke the old Flores trope, those issues are the “takes no talent” stuff that should be improving. If I was Hafley, I would have those guys puking their guts out running gassers back and forth to the TNT wall for those penalties. It needs to stop. THERE YOU ARE! You were hiding all along, and we thought you had disappeared. But you came back. I’m, of course, talking about the offensive line we have come to know and hate over the years. Willis was sacked 3 times – I saw 2 of them – and those, I would argue, are due to his inability to escape like he wants to. But he was under assault all game long. He had several where he was flushed from the pocket and couldn’t find an open pass catcher. Austin Jackson was particularly atrocious, and Slowik’s decision to have him go one-on-one with a premier pass rusher defies logic. That hurt the game plan and may have killed any trade value he had. Paul seemed to have a decent day, but everyone else struggled, and it was pretty rough to watch. Will Kacmarek had a rough game. He nullified the huge pass play to Coleman. Then he had a terrible sequence in the 2nd half where he had a false start on 2nd down, then dropped a 3rd-down pass that would have converted. The Dolphins converted the fake punt play right after that, so they stayed on the field. But that was a bad stretch. He was known as a limited but reliable receiver in college. Can’t have those big drops with limited opportunities. Both Douglas and Coleman look like keepers. Douglas is the big-time playmaker, but Coleman has stepped it up. He only had one target, but it was a huge play. Well, it should have been a huge play. Bell remains quiet, and concerns about his ability to create separation are growing. I remain firm in the belief that he is a big slot player. But right now, he isn’t stepping up like his rookie counterparts. Bradley Pinion had the best pass of the game for the Dolphins on the fake punt play. But the shanked punt gave the Lions great field position that led to points. The defense forced a FG, but it was a 40-yard FG. Imagine if the punt had been 45 yards instead of 25. If the same play sequence occurs, the Lions may be forced to kick a 60-yarder instead. Or perhaps they go for it on 4th-and-10. Or maybe they punt. Not that it mattered, because the Dolphins took the ball, marched down the field, and attempted a FGto tie the game at halftime. Gonzalez doinked the kick off the upright. Now, that 6-point swing didn’t necessarily affect the outcome. But look at that sequence of events. A shanked punt led to field position and 3 points from Detroit, giving them a 6-3 lead. What if they don’t get those points because the Dolphins’ defense steps up after a better punt? What if Gonzalez hits that FG and the Dolphins get a 3-point lead going into the half? Again, it’s little mistakes like the poor punt, missed FG, and penalties that can affect the margins, and the Dolphins have to win the margins to have a chance. I can be lenient with rookies like Kacmarek. But Gonzalez and Pinion are literally the oldest players on the Dolphins’ field. That is simply unacceptable performance for those players. Gonzalez has had his 3rd call-up from the practice squad, and the team will have to decide whether to add him to the 53-man roster or let him walk. At this point, I would try out some young kickers and let them have a chance. Who cares if they miss or if they suck? It’s about seeing what kind of gems the team can unearth. Maybe they find a stud kicker. Maybe not. But Gonzalez ain’t it, and neither is Pinion. The Dolphins are 1-7. There is no use…

title: Kirk Cousins Returns: Vikings Rescue Plan or Costly Gamble?
summary: Kirk Cousins returns to the Minnesota Vikings—but can this trade save their season? On this bonus episode of The Real Forno Show, host Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano examine the quarterback reunion, its third-round draft cost, and the pressure facing Kevin O’Connell. This Vikings 1st & SKOL discussion balances immediate hope with long-term consequences: […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 8: Kirk Cousins #8 of the Las Vegas Raiders warms up prior to an NFL football game against the San Francisco 49ers at Levi's Stadium on November 8, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Kirk Cousins returns to the Minnesota Vikings —but can this trade save their season? On this bonus episode of The Real Forno Show , host Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano examine the quarterback reunion, its third-round draft cost, and the pressure facing Kevin O’Connell. This Vikings 1st & SKOL discussion balances immediate hope with long-term consequences: Minnesota needs competent offense to support a defense playing winning football. Forness doesn’t soften his assessment of the price: “The Vikings got fleeced.” Yet Stefano sees a necessary response to an offense struggling to sustain drives: “He gives us the best chance at winning ballgames.” The Kirk Cousins trade debate centers on familiarity versus desperation. Forness explains that Cousins already understands O’Connell’s system and has established chemistry with Justin Jefferson, making him a logical option after Kyler Murray’s injury and Carson Wentz’s struggles. The hosts argue that Minnesota’s quarterback problems reflect a series of decisions involving J.J. McCarthy, Sam Darnold, and Daniel Jones—not one isolated mistake. Reviewing Cousins’ Raiders production, Forness cites 2,340 passing yards, 20 touchdowns, eight interceptions, and a 97.1 passer rating. Those numbers offer encouragement, but concerns remain about the 38-year-old quarterback’s late-season stamina, an inconsistent running game, and future salary-cap obligations. Forness gives the deal a C+, explaining, “It was a move they had to make,” while maintaining that Minnesota paid too much. His ultimate measuring stick is straightforward: “If you make a playoff run, it’s worth a third round pick.” Key points from the episode: A familiar quarterback, a faster transition: Cousins’ knowledge of the offense and receivers could help Minnesota stabilize without an extensive learning period. Justin Jefferson needs opportunities: The hosts emphasize getting the ball to Minnesota’s star receiver and avoiding further offensive frustration. The defense deserves support: Forness argues that making a move signals belief in a unit that has continued to compete against strong offenses. The financial cost extends beyond the trade: Forness discusses a $10 million impact on Minnesota’s 2027 cap and the possibility of renegotiating Cousins’ contract. Kevin O’Connell faces greater scrutiny: “It doesn’t matter how good your offense can look, it’s whether or not your team can execute it,” Forness says. He raises coaching accountability as a possibility, not a prediction of a firing. No running back reinforcement arrived: Jonathan Taylor and Tony Pollard enter the discussion as potential solutions, but the deadline passes without a backfield addition. Locker-room morale matters: Forness references Alec Lewis’ reporting that players were excited about Cousins’ return. Listen: View Link Or on your favorite podcast aggregator. Watch or listen to The Real Forno Show with Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano on Vikings 1st & SKOL for the full debate, detailed analysis, and candid fan conversation. This Minnesota Vikings podcast asks whether familiar quarterback play can unlock an offense with talent around it, or merely postpone bigger decisions. Fan with Us!!! title: A Plea from an Idiot: Please let “Kirko Chainz” be a thing of the past
summary: I’ve written about Minnesota sports for almost two decades, and before that I was a slightly worse-than-mediocre high school athlete. I guess I played an inning of Division III baseball, too. One thing I’ve always shied away from is normalizing my “experience” as any part of my analysis of any sport. Me hitting .253 in […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - DECEMBER 31: Injured quarterback Kirk Cousins #8 of the Minnesota Vikings and his son fire up the crowd prior to the game against the Green Bay Packers at U.S. Bank Stadium on December 31, 2023 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images I’ve written about Minnesota sports for almost two decades, and before that I was a slightly worse-than-mediocre high school athlete. I guess I played an inning of Division III baseball, too. One thing I’ve always shied away from is normalizing my “experience” as any part of my analysis of any sport. Me hitting .253 in the spring of 2004 doesn’t mean I intrinsically know why Royce Lewis has fallen off in the last few seasons. Now, could I do a little math or look into some data and try to figure out why? Sure. But I will almost never say “well this is what I saw or how I did it” as justification for one of my #takes. I’m going to change course on that for one second here. The Minnesota Vikings announced that they’d acquired Kirk Cousins for their original 2027 third-round draft pick — not the pick the team acquired from Philadelphia for Jonathan Greenard (a pick that will likely convey a bit better than the team’s original pick). We all remember the fun and memes and whatnot from Kirk’s first go-round with the team. Kirko Chainz was the big one. It was fun. It really was. The whitest guy you ever saw play football was acting exactly the opposite of how you’d expect. View Link In a way, it was like Joe Mauer walking up to T.I’s “What You Know” for all those years. But if there’s one thing I remember from my youth, it’s that jokes and gags don’t age well. They don’t transfer well from year to year. If your football team has a running inside joke or something one year, my experience has always been that the joke does not make a return in subsequent seasons. It’s cringy. It becomes lore. But it absolutely dies — a humane death. The Twins did not do this with the Bomba Squad after 2019, and it just….wasn’t good. The Bomba Siren sounded long after Eddie Rosario — who initially coined the phrase — had left the Twins and been on multiple subsequent teams. The 2019 team set records for most home runs hit in a season — and haven’t come close since. In fact, as I recall, the one thing that didn’t hang around was playing Rage Against the Machine’s “Bombtrack” as the song for when the hitter rounded the bases — similar to the Star Wars theme back in the mid-90s when I first started watching the Twins. That was objectively the one good thing that should have hung around from the Bomba Squad, because Bombtrack after hitting a bomb just sounds cool, and if you line it up right, it jives nicely with the average home run trot. For example (this also lines up kinda nicely for the Kirk gif above, I might add): Listen: I’m just some random idiot. I have no delusions about my value to this general space *gestures everywhere* . I just think it’s time to let Kirko Chainz die — and let a new bit rise up from the ashes in its place. Learn from the mistakes of your former roommates and don’t let an otherwise cool(ish) meme become cringy.

title: Welcome Back Kirko!
summary: After a horrible performance by Carson Wentz capping off a half-season of poor performing quarterback play, the Minnesota Vikings are bringing back Kirk Cousins to lead the offense for the rest of the season. In exchange, the Vikings are sending their third-round pick (not the one from the Eagles) in the 2027 draft to Las […]
full_text: Oct 14, 2018; Minneapolis, MN, USA; Minnesota Vikings quarterback Kirk Cousins (8) celebrates his touchdown during the third quarter against the Arizona Cardinals at U.S. Bank Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Brace Hemmelgarn-USA TODAY Sports After a horrible performance by Carson Wentz capping off a half-season of poor performing quarterback play, the Minnesota Vikings are bringing back Kirk Cousins to lead the offense for the rest of the season. In exchange, the Vikings are sending their third-round pick (not the one from the Eagles) in the 2027 draft to Las Vegas. Cousins will have minimal impact on the Vikings’ 2026 salary cap ($650K) but is due a roster bonus of $10 million next year. The Vikings and then GM Kwesi Adofo-Mensah balked at Cousins’ demands for a contract extension back in 2024, as they were planning to draft a quarterback high that year- and did in J.J. McCarthy- and opted for Sam Darnold as a bridge option. Cousins ultimately got double-crossed by the Atlanta Falcons, who gave Cousins a big contract but also drafted Michael Penix in the first round and ultimately ate a lot of Cousins’ contract as he struggled in the year after his Achilles tear. He eventually was signed by the Raiders this year as a bridge to their top draft pick, Fernando Mendoza. He has played well this year, ranking 10th in EPA/play, right there with the rest of the quarterbacks in the NFC North. Cousins was quarterback the last time the Vikings won a playoff game- in 2019. This is the second time the Vikings were ‘only a quarterback away’ from competing for a championship, but with the way the Vikings defense is playing and the rest of the supporting cast on offense, that may be more true now than it was back in 2018 when Cousins was originally signed. Now the question will be how quickly Cousins can reacclimate to the Vikings offense. My guess is that the Vikings and Cousins will do everything they can to have him start on Sunday against the Packers at Lambeau Field, which is where he played his last game as a Viking in his first stint with the Vikings. The acquisition of Cousins will be just the balm the Vikings need after suffering two defeats that easily could have been victories with decent quarterback play. Now the Vikings should have at least decent quarterback play with Cousins at the helm, and be in a better position to reclaim the lead in the division by the end of the season and make a run in the playoffs with good injury luck. Welcome back Kirko! Here are highlights from Kirk’s first stint with the Vikings for your viewing pleasure. Follow me on X/Bluesky @wludford

full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 08: Kirk Cousins #8 of the Las Vegas Raiders throws a pass during the first quarter against the San Francisco 49ers at Levi's Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) | Getty Images Ladies and gentlemen. . .they got him. According to Adam Schefter of ESPN, the Minnesota Vikings and the Las Vegas Raiders are finalizing the terms of a deal that will send quarterback Kirk Cousins back to the Vikings. The Vikings will, reportedly, send a third-round pick to the Raiders in exchange for Cousins. Cousins started 88 games for the Vikings from 2018 to 2023. During that time, he completed 67.9% of his passes for 23,265 yards, which is third in franchise history behind Fran Tarkenton and Tommy Kramer (he’s only about 1,500 yards behind Kramer). He also threw 171 touchdown passes to 55 interceptions while compiling a 50-37-1 record as a starter. In Cousins’ one full season in Kevin O’Connell’s offense, Cousins completed 65.9% of his passes for 4,549 yards, 29 touchdowns, and 14 interceptions. The Vikings also put up a record of 13-4 that season despite a defense coordinated by Ed Donatell that couldn’t stop a nosebleed. They won the NFC North that season but lost on Wild Card Weekend to the New York Giants. Now, he has the backing of Brian Flores’ defense. One can’t help but feel that things might be just a little bit better with that combination in Minnesota. The Vikings have two third-round picks in the 2027 NFL Draft: Theirs and the pick they’ll be receiving from the Philadelphia Eagles in the Jonathan Greenard trade. No word at this time which pick they’ll be sending to the Raiders, though one would assume it would be the better of those two picks, which is currently Philadelphia’s. If we do get some clarification we’ll pass it along. UPDATE : The pick is the Vikings’ own third-rounder, which currently sits about twenty spots lower than the one they’ll be getting from the Eagles as things stand right now, so my earlier assumption was incorrect. We’ve taken the liberty of providing a first look at what Cousins will look like in his new Vikings uniform. Man. . .the things you can do with computers these days, huh? Kirk Cousins is back, folks. So, let me ask you. . .do you like that?

full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 08: Kirk Cousins #8 of the Las Vegas Raiders looks to pass against the San Francisco 49ers in the fourth quarter of an NFL football game at Levi's Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images With a little more than two hours to go before the NFL Trade Deadline, the Minnesota Vikings are looking for a quarterback. While this is not really news. . .particularly if you watched whatever the hell that was we subjected ourselves to on Monday night. . .we have gotten some news on who their primary target appears to be. Vikings have identified Raiders QB Kirk Cousins as a prime trade candidate ahead of today’s 4 pm ET deadline, per league sources. The clock is ticking to get a deal done. pic.twitter.com/xn4ol0Yq6G — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) November 10, 2026 According to Adam Schefter of ESPN, the Vikings have reportedly identified Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins as a primary target for a trade acquisition. Cousins, of course, spent six seasons with the Vikings from 2018 to 2023, and it was his Achilles injury in 2023 that basically launched the quarterback odyssey that the Vikings currently find themselves on. After Cousins’ injury, the Vikings chose not to re-sign him before the 2024 season, and he moved on to the Atlanta Falcons. That led to the team bringing Sam Darnold in as a free agent and drafting J.J. McCarthy in the 2024 NFL Draft, which led to Darnold taking the job after McCarthy’s preseason injury and. . .well, I’m not going to rehash the entire timeline here, but it’s been mostly bad since then. The Raiders are currently in third place in the AFC West with a 4-5 record, and Cousins has thrown 20 touchdown passes so far this season. Of all the potentially available options, Cousins is the one who likely gives the Vikings the best chance of a boost this season because of his familiarity with the Vikings’ system and the fact that. . .well, he can actually complete a forward pass, which would be a big step forward from where the offense currently is now. The question remains whether or not the Raiders want to move Cousins or not. At 4-5, they are still in contention in the AFC, but they do have this year’s #1 overall pick, Fernando Mendoza, waiting in the wings. They obviously want to build around him for the future, and the price they could likely extract from the Vikings for Cousins’ services could be a boost towards helping them to do that. What do you think, folks? Is it time for a Kirk Cousins reunion in Minnesota? Talk about it in the comments, and we’ll be keeping our eyes on the wire to see if anything happens between now and 3:00 PM Central Time.

Carson Wentz Wentz would’ve been more accurate if he was blindfolded last night. He consistently missed throws by 10+ yards. He’s had two starts this year and the team has score 15 points combined. title: Vikings vs. Packers odds: Opening lines for Week 10 matchup
summary: After falling out of first place in the NFC North for the first time this season, the Minnesota Vikings will look to avoid moving into the division’s basement when they head to Lambeau Field in Week 10 to conclude their home-and-home series with the Green Bay Packers for this season. The people who set the […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - NOVEMBER 09: Christian Benford #47 of the Buffalo Bills breaks up a pass intended for Justin Jefferson #18 of the Minnesota Vikings during the first quarter of the game at U.S. Bank Stadium on November 09, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images After falling out of first place in the NFC North for the first time this season, the Minnesota Vikings will look to avoid moving into the division’s basement when they head to Lambeau Field in Week 10 to conclude their home-and-home series with the Green Bay Packers for this season. The people who set the betting lines, apparently, don’t like their chances. Our friends at the FanDuel Sportsbook have opened the lines for Sunday’s game, and the Vikings currently sit as a 4.5-point underdog to the Packers. The over/under for the game currently rests at 42.5 points. The Vikings, as we all saw on Monday Night Football, appear to have completely abandoned the concept of offense, as they generated none of it in a 23-6 loss to the Buffalo Bills for their second loss in a row. Carson Wentz stepped in at quarterback for the injured Kyler Murray and turned in what may have been the worst start a Vikings quarterback has put together in recent memory, completing just 8-of-25 passes and turning the ball over three times, including two interceptions. . .a number that could have been significantly higher. The Packers, on the other hand, have won five of their last six after getting off to a 1-2 start. This past week, they absolutely thumped the New England Patriots to the tune of 45-27 behind three more touchdown passes from Jordan Love and a defense that forced Drake Maye into three interceptions. The Packers currently sit in last place in the North, but with a 6-3 record would lead either the NFC South or the NFC East. . .that’s just how good the NFC North has been this season. These two teams met in the regular season opener at U.S. Bank Stadium. Wentz came into the game midway through the first quarter after Murray suffered a concussion, and the Packers had a 22-10 lead with just over five minutes remaining in the third quarter. From there, however, the Minnesota defense took over, leading an onslaught against Love and the Green Bay offense that saw the Vikings score 29 unanswered points to finish the game, including forcing a turnover on downs and generating an interception and a fumble to set up scoring opportunities. Minnesota took home the 39-22 win to get their season off to a 1-0 start. With the NFL trade deadline looming at 3:00 PM Central today. . .or approximately seven hours from when this story goes up. . .we will see if anything the Vikings do (or don’t do) will shift this number at all. As it stands now, however, the Vikings are currently an underdog to their division rivals as the second half of the season officially gets underway.

title: Patriots to face Kirk Cousins a second time after trade to Vikings
summary: With the NFL trade deadline nearing, the New England Patriots have been quiet. The same cannot be said for one of their opponents. The Minnesota Vikings, who will visit the Patriots in Week 14 for a prime time matchup, have acquired quarterback Kirk Cousins from the Las Vegas Raiders. Cousins already spent six seasons in […]
full_text: With the NFL trade deadline nearing, the New England Patriots have been quiet. The same cannot be said for one of their opponents. The Minnesota Vikings, who will visit the Patriots in Week 14 for a prime time matchup, have acquired quarterback Kirk Cousins from the Las Vegas Raiders. Cousins already spent six seasons in Minnesota between 2018 and 2023. As confirmed by the Vikings, they are sending a third-round selection in next year’s draft to Las Vegas to complete the trade. Cousins, 38, started all nine of the Raiders’ games so far this season. One of those came against the Patriots: in Week 5, he completed 19 of 28 pass attempts for 243 yards with a touchdown and three sacks. Despite him posting some solid overall stats, Las Vegas was blown out by a final score of 45-17. Cousins will now join a Vikings team that started the season 6-0 but has dropped back-to-back contests while struggling to get competent quarterback play out of the trio of Kyler Murray, Carson Wentz and Max Brosmer. The low point came on Monday night against the Bills, when Wentz went 8-for-25 for 81 yards and a pair of interceptions in a 23-6 defeat. If all goes according to Minnesota’s plans, however, none of those three will be under center come the mid-December game in Foxborough. Instead, Cousins, as pointed out by Ethan Hurwitz of Patriots on SI, is on track to become one of only eight quarterbacks in NFL history to have faced the same team twice a season while wearing different teams’ uniforms. When New England last played the Vikings back in 2022, Cousins also was their starting quarterback. He led his team to a 33-26 win against the Mac Jones-led Patriots.

title: 3-Point Stance: Patriots’ trade deadline isn’t time for a youth movement
summary: Are the New England Patriots sellers at the NFL trade deadline? On Nov. 1, Sports Illustrated’s Albert Breer highlighted defensive tackle Christian Barmore and cornerback Carlton Davis as potential Patriots trade candidates ahead of Tuesday’s deadline at 4 p.m. According to Breer, if a deal is struck, New England’s motivation would be centered around adding […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - NOVEMBER 8: Christian Watson #9 of the Green Bay Packers makes a catch against Carlton Davis III #7 of the New England Patriots during an NFL football game at Gillette Stadium on November 8, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Are the New England Patriots sellers at the NFL trade deadline? On Nov. 1, Sports Illustrated’s Albert Breer highlighted defensive tackle Christian Barmore and cornerback Carlton Davis as potential Patriots trade candidates ahead of Tuesday’s deadline at 4 p.m. According to Breer, if a deal is struck, New England’s motivation would be centered around adding draft capital and transitioning into a younger roster. As of Nov. 4, head coach Mike Vrabel appeared to disagree with that approach. “I think sometimes national reports have the tendency to do that. I have not shared that information with anybody,” Vrabel said. “This time of year, I think that all these things kind of get drummed up. So, we’re focused on trying to prepare for [the Green Bay Packers] and make the corrections from [the week before]. “This is business as normal here, so I don’t know where a lot of these things come from. Certainly not from any conversations with me.” However, does Vrabel and Co.’s stance about handling the trade deadline change after New England’s brutal 45-27 loss at the hands of the Packers on Sunday? Vrabel offered a simple response when making an appearance on WEEI’s The Greg Hill Show : “No.” “We want a bunch of guys that want to be here,” he added. “That want to make it hard on each other. In preparation, push each other, challenge each other, improve, take accountability, and if that’s not them, then let us know by tomorrow. That’s what we have to do. That’s the mindset.” And from a selling standpoint, his ruling could make sense as a final decision. Regardless of whether or not the Patriots strike a deal involving either Barmore or Davis, trading almost any impact contributor on the roster while sitting at a 5-4 record at the regular season’s midway point, especially in the AFC, is certainly questionable. Both players were also members of the tight-knit group that made a Super Bowl appearance just nine months ago. At the least, a deal of that stature calls for a corresponding “buying” move. Sure, New England’s depth in multiple areas will be a largely discussed topic throughout the offseason regarding the team’s roster-building process. And rightfully so. Vrabel said it himself after a preseason victory over the Philadelphia Eagles, stating at the time that he doesn’t think his team is “very deep.” But six 2027 day-three draft picks make finding immediate, injury-relieving depth manageable. Sending away either Barmore or Davis simply doesn’t make sense at this time. Especially for a franchise still technically in contention for the AFC East title. Trading Barmore creates another need In 2023, Barmore posted his best season as a pro, recording 8.5 sacks, 16 quarterback hits and pressuring those passers 49 times. He also consistently disrupted opposing run offenses, forcing 13 tackles for a loss and totaling 64 combined takedowns. That season-long performance earned the Patriots’ 2021 second-round draft selection a four-year, $84 million contract extension the following offseason. Currently in year two of that new deal, Barmore’s production hasn’t entirely matched the monetary value of his contract, especially in run defense. From just last season, the 27-year-old has seen his involvement in that facet of the defense drop from 62.8% to just 36%. Still, New England evidently continues to view Barmore as a producer when rushing the quarterback, heavily using the defensive tackle during pass-rush downs and critical third-down plays. Barmore’s overall reduced role also doesn’t mean he’s expendable. Trading him shuffles the defensive line, forcing Cory Durden into a new, pass-rush-heavy role and 34-year-old DaQuan Jones, who has contributed as a relief piece for the primary starters, into a heavier workload. Davis’ departure would leave a hole in the secondary As for Davis, the cornerback hasn’t shown signs of regression. But the soon-to-be 30-year-old, entering the final year of his contract with a mighty injury history and owed $22 million in 2027, plays directly into the youth-movement argument. Nonetheless, shipping him off to another franchise creates a glaring hole in the cornerback room. That decision then forces Vrabel and the defensive coaching staff to decide between starting substitute Charles Woods opposite Christian Gonzalez or pulling Marcus Jones away from his natural nickel-cornerback position. With several offenses in the Patriots’ remaining schedule currently ranking top 10 in passing yards per game, that potential decision seems counterproductive. Davis, who recently returned to the starting lineup last week after missing four games, played a significant role in New England’s divisional round victory against the Houston Texans in the playoffs last season, intercepting C.J. Stroud twice. The offseason offers a better time to make a move In Barmore’s case, an eventual deal appears likely. As the Boston Herald’s Andrew Callahan put it , the Patriots seemingly want “out of the Barmore business.” On Friday, Breer wrote that the price for both Barmore and Davis “would likely” be around just a fourth-round selection. An offseason deal, rather than a midseason trade, allows New England greater flexibility to reallocate resources and explore replacements to replicate or improve upon either player’s production while spending less. The Patriots’ loss to Green Bay is concerning. Still, it’s not a season-ending sign. It’s true that New England’s defense has struggled to deliver on the expectations surrounding their offseason additions of Dre’Mont Jones, All-Pro safety Kevin Byard and second-round pick Gabe Jacas. But much like the rest of the roster, that group has dealt with injuries. The team’s matchup against the Miami Dolphins in Week Eight marked the first game the starting cornerback trio of Gonzalez, Davis and Jones all played together since Week Three. Even though eventually moving Barmore or another established contributor makes sense for the team’s long-term roster construction, the Patriots’ timing of a potential trade should account for the franchise’s current position in the AFC playoff picture.

I’m not ready to declare the roster a sinking ship yet though. This also happens to be the NFL trade deadline, today at 4:00 pm ET. I’ve heard many fans bemoaning the fact that the front office isn’t doing anything to try and add pieces to patch up the roster. If the issue is shoring up one position, then the price may be worth it to sail on to the playoffs. But where would the Patriots even start? OL? RB? WR? The list is too long. title: 6 potential Patriots targets ahead of the NFL trade deadline
summary: The Nov. 10 4 p.m. ET NFL trade deadline is just hours away. Despite being just days removed from an ugly loss, the 5-4 New England Patriots still view themselves as contenders which could impact how they manage the roster. “I want to see us do anything that we can with the roster that we […]
full_text: The Nov. 10 4 p.m. ET NFL trade deadline is just hours away. Despite being just days removed from an ugly loss, the 5-4 New England Patriots still view themselves as contenders which could impact how they manage the roster. “I want to see us do anything that we can with the roster that we have or potentially guys that aren’t here, to continue to improve,” head coach Mike Vrabel said Monday. “That’s the focus here after nine weeks. We played some really good games, have been competitive, and then other days where it just wasn’t good enough as a whole.” After trading a 2028 first-round pick this past offseason, the Patriots are not expected to make any significant investments. But the team does have additional Day 3 draft capital this year to add depth across the roster. As for potential targets, here are six targets who could be on the radar. DT Roy Lopez The Patriots’ run defense has trended in a positive direction in recent weeks, but adding Lopez could help the unit take another step forward. The 29-year-old has shown flashes of being a dominant run defender along the interior and would give New England another reliable option in the defensive line rotation. He is also under contract through the 2027 season for a reasonable salary. DT Dalvin Tomlinson Another option along the interior defensive line, Tomlinson has lost some of the pass-rushing juice he showed earlier in his career but remains a disruptive rotational piece. The 32-year-old is in the final year of his contract with the winless Chargers, with roughly $1.5 million remaining in cash owed to him. That makes him a potentially affordable option compared to Colts nose tackle Grover Stewart, who is owed approximately $6 million in cash. Tomlinson also spent the 2024 season with Mike Vrabel in Cleveland. ED Zaven Collins The Patriots have gotten strong overall production from Elijah Ponder, Dre’Mont Jones and Gabe Jacas along the edge. However, adding another pass rusher could help preserve that production down the stretch and bring some more juice to the unit as a whole. The former first-round pick, who has the size and athleticism New England has gravitated to on the edge, has served in a rotational role for the Cardinals this season and is in the final year of his contract, potentially making him an attainable deadline target. ED Nolan Smith The 2-7 Eagles continued to move pieces ahead of the trade deadline Monday, sending defensive tackle Jordan Davis to Jacksonville in exchange for a first- and second-round pick. Could former first-round pick Nolan Smith be next? Despite the Eagles’ struggles, the 25-year-old has been productive, leading the team with 21 pressures this season while remaining a physical run defender. Philadelphia also exercised Smith’s fifth-year option this past offseason, keeping him under contract through 2027 with under $14 million in cash owed his way. His age, production and contractual control could make him an appealing addition, although it may take a more significant investment than other names on this list. CB Jonathan Jones New England’s secondary was already without cornerback Charles Woods (hamstring) Sunday before fellow cornerback Carlton Davis (knee) left the game early. That left Christian Gonzalez and Marcus Jones with limited depth behind them, as rookies Karon Prunty and Channing Canada were the next options at cornerback. Former Patriot Jonathan Jones has settled into a rotational role with the Eagles, but still offers experience and man-coverage ability that could be valuable for a New England secondary dealing with injuries. Draft capital As noted above, the Patriots are without their 2028 first-round pick after sending it to Philadelphia in the offseason trade for A.J. Brown. While New England is focused on competing this season, there is still a bigger-picture argument for adding draft capital and getting younger across the roster. That probably is more of an offseason focus, but the team could explore the trade market to potentially move a veteran on the current roster if the right offer comes along.
author: Brian Hines

title: Patriots injury analysis after Packers loss in Week 9
summary: The New England Patriots suffered one of their worst losses in recent memory against the Green Bay Packers on Sunday. Not only were they beaten with a final score of 45-27, they also saw multiple players go down with injuries. While not all of those were equally serious, some are a definitive cause for concern. […]
full_text: The New England Patriots suffered one of their worst losses in recent memory against the Green Bay Packers on Sunday. Not only were they beaten with a final score of 45-27 , they also saw multiple players go down with injuries. While not all of those were equally serious, some are a definitive cause for concern. After rewatching the game, let’s go through what is an extensive list for a team that has struggled with injuries all year long. Patriots injury analysis: NFL Week 9 S Brenden Schooler: Already nursing a hamstring issue entering the game, Schooler was limited to just four snaps against the Packers — all within the game’s first five minutes. The final one came on a Mitch Wishnowsky punt in the first quarter, and did not see the team captain suffer any obvious injury while working his typical role as a gunner. His hamstring still prevented him form finishing the game. CB Carlton Davis III: While teammate Christian Gonzalez broke up a fourth-down pass late in the second quarter, Carlton Davis came up limping after making a cut in coverage against Packers receiver Christian Watson. He remained down on one knee on the sideline, and eventually slowly made his way to the blue medical tent. Davis was later announced as questionable to return with a knee injury, and ultimately ruled out instead of reentering the contest. LG Ben Brown: Getting spun around while sustaining a pass block in the late second quarter, Brown went down after the play and received medical attention on the field. He slowly walked off under his own power and was later announced as questionable to reenter the contest with a knee issue. He too never came back. TE Cameron Latu: Latu remained on the ground after a kickoff return in the late third quarter; he was taken down from behind while holding his block for returner Corey Kiner. He eventually jogged off the field and returned for the next special teams opportunity three minutes of game time later. No injury was announced by the team. RB Rhamondre Stevenson: Catching a short pass near the sideline with under four minutes to go in the third quarter, Stevenson attempted to get up as normal but ultimately hobbled and went back down. He received some assistance by the Patriots medical staff, but walked off under his own power and into the medical tent. He departed for the locker room shortly thereafter and was quickly ruled out for the remainder of the game because of a knee injury. S Jaylen Reed: The Patriots’ No. 3 safety took a brief trip to the blue medical tent in the late third quarter, but remained on the sidelines and reentered the contest shortly thereafter. As with Cameron Latu, no injury was announced for Reed either. LT Will Campbell: Early in the fourth quarter, New England’s starting left tackle went down after blitzing safety Evan Williams collided with him from behind. Dealing with a knee injury, he walked off with members of the Patriots training staff and into the blue medical tent. The Patriots announced him as questionable to return, and he finished the game on the sidelines. QB Drake Maye: The Patriots’ starting quarterback took a hard fall on a 10-yard sack with 10 minutes to go in the game. He was a bit slow to get up and eventually pulled from the game, although the decision to remove him had to do with the score at that point — 45-21 — as well as an overall attempt to preserve him rather than any effects from that particular play. WR Kyle Williams: Williams came up limping after an incomplete target in the late fourth quarter (that ultimately did not count anyway due to a roughing-the-passer penalty). He was not on the field for the next two plays, but returned for the two-point conversion after a Corey Kiner touchdown run. The ball again came his way, was not completed, and he was shaken up: the second-year receiver took a hard fall while trying to reach for the overthrown pass. He returned for the game’s final two snaps. What this means for the Patriots As if losing by 18 points wasn’t bad enough, the already injury-plagued Patriots also took some more hits on Sunday. Not all of them appear to be of the major variety, but some certainly are. Rhamondre Stevenson, for example, is reportedly set to miss some time due to a knee tendon injury. Ben Brown, meanwhile, won’t be available for the team against the Detroit Lions in Germany on Sunday. The statuses of Carlton Davis and Brenden Schooler, who also were unable to finish the contest, remain to be determined — as will any other effects from the game. It wasn’t all bad news, though. Will Campbell, for example, said after the game that he could have returned had the score not been out of hand at that point. Still, the Patriots will once again be forced to adapt. At running back, this means potentially being down the top two options this week versus the Lions. Besides Stevenson, TreVeyon Henderson has now missed back-to-back games because of an illness of undetermined origin . This means that Corey Kiner, Lan Larison and practice squad option Terrell Jennings would remain as the only available backs in Week 10. Along the offensive line, meanwhile, the Patriots’ turnover at guard is set to continue. With Brown out, the team will either reinsert Walter Rouse or veteran Greg Van Roten, whose window to return from injured reserve was opened last week. The Patriots will hold their first practice of the week on Wednesday before taking an overnight flight to Munich. They will then hold a light session on Thursday followed by another regular practice on Friday. Kickoff against the Lions is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. ET on Sunday.

title: Patriots playoff picture after loss to Packers in Week 9
summary: Coming off a Super Bowl berth, the New England Patriots entered the 2026 season with some high expectations. Those have not changed, but Sunday’s 45-27 loss to the Green Bay Packers showed that meeting them might become even more of a challenge than initially anticipated. What will happen over the coming weeks and months remains […]
full_text: Coming off a Super Bowl berth, the New England Patriots entered the 2026 season with some high expectations. Those have not changed, but Sunday’s 45-27 loss to the Green Bay Packers showed that meeting them might become even more of a challenge than initially anticipated. What will happen over the coming weeks and months remains to be seen, of course, but for now let’s focus on the concrete impact that defeat had on the standings. AFC East standings Buffalo Bills (7-1) New England Patriots (5-4) New York Jets (2-7) Miami Dolphins (1-7) The Patriots defending their AFC East title will be a challenge, even though they own the head-to-head advantage over the Bills courtesy of their Week 4 victory in Buffalo. However, what good is that advantage if you cannot get even in the standings? And with New England falling to 5-4 and the Bills winning their seventh game on Monday night against the Vikings, doing so will be tough. Not only will the Patriots need the Bills to start dropping some games to overcome their current 2.5-point deficit, they themself also cannot allow many more slip-ups. Considering that five of their final eight opponents currently reside in either the AFC or NFC playoff pictures, that is far from a given. Elsewhere in the AFC East Week 9 was business as usual. The Jets lost 35-12 to the Chiefs and are inching closer toward rebuild category once more, while the Dolphins — whose lone win this season came against New York — were once again unable to make enough plays to prevent a 19-9 loss to the Lions. AFC playoff standings Buffalo Bills (7-1) Denver Broncos (7-2) Jacksonville Jaguars (6-2) Pittsburgh Steelers (6-2) Kansas City Chiefs (6-2) Cincinnati Bengals (6-2) New England Patriots (5-4) On the bubble: 8. Cleveland Browns (5-4) , 9. Las Vegas Raiders (4-5), 10. Baltimore Ravens (4-5), 11. Houston Texans (3- 5) Not yet eliminated, but let’s be real here: 12. New York Jets (2-7), 13. Indianapolis Colts (2-7), 14. Miami Dolphins (1-7), 15. Tennessee Titans (1-7), 16. Los Angeles Chargers (0-8) Even though they were dominated on Sunday, the Patriots still remain in the driver’s seat for a playoff spot in the AFC. They do have multiple advantages over the only other 5-4 team in the conference, the Browns. New England’s conference record is superior, while it also owns the strength of victory and strength of schedule tiebreakers at the moment. With no head-to-head matchup on the schedule, those tiebreakers might decide who makes it to the postseason when all is said and done. Of course, there is still a long way to go before any conversations about the playoffs become serious. For the time being, though, the Patriots are still in control of their own destiny even if they ended up ceding more ground to the other wild card competitors. NFC playoff standings San Francisco 49ers (7-1) Chicago Bears (7-2) New York Giants (5-2-1) Carolina Panthers (3-5) Detroit Lions (6-2) Minnesota Vikings (6-2) Green Bay Packers (6-3) On the bubble: 8. title: Saints RB Audric Estime makes Browns pay for letting him go
summary: Sometimes the NFL writes the perfect script, and Audric Estime could not have asked for a better opportunity to make a statement. After being waived by the Cleveland Browns earlier in the week, Estime found himself back home after the New Orleans Saints claimed him on waivers, playing a significant role in the recent victory […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - NOVEMBER 08: Audric Estimé #30 of the New Orleans Saints carries the ball against the Cleveland Browns during the first half of the NFL football game at Cesars Superdome on November 8, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Sometimes the NFL writes the perfect script, and Audric Estime could not have asked for a better opportunity to make a statement. After being waived by the Cleveland Browns earlier in the week, Estime found himself back home after the New Orleans Saints claimed him on waivers, playing a significant role in the recent victory against his former club. Estime finished with 15 carries for 72 yards and a big-time touchdown, giving the Saints a much-needed boost in the backfield amid their run game struggles. The Browns had an opportunity to keep Estime after he impressed in his lone appearance with them but ultimately decided to move on. Just days later, he was helping the Saints secure a win against them. It’s difficult to imagine a more fitting way for a player to respond after not being rewarded for his production. For the Saints, Estime’s performance also raised an important question about whether they moved on from him too quickly. With the recent release of Kendre Miller, Estime being around earlier in the season could have been beneficial to New Orleans’ rushing attack. Estime didn’t need a heavy workload to make his presence felt, but his contributions made a difference, especially when the offense has been looking for someone to step up in the backfield. There is still plenty of football left to play, and one strong performance doesn’t guarantee Estime maintain this trajectory moving forward. However, he’s proven to make the most of his opportunities each time he steps on the field, no matter the uniform he’s sporting. He certainly made the most of his opportunity against Cleveland.

title: Saints vs. Browns: The good, the bad, and the ugly in Week 9
summary: The Good: Pass Rush The New Orleans Saints pass rush did a great job getting to Shedeur Sanders on Sunday, sacking the second-year quarterback five times while also getting three additional tackles for loss. Carl Granderson sacked Sanders twice and Chase Young sacked him once. Both players now rank in the top 3 in the […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - NOVEMBER 08: Shedeur Sanders #2 of the Cleveland Browns is sacked by Carl Granderson #96 of the New Orleans Saints during the third quarter at Caesars Superdome on November 08, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Good: Pass Rush The New Orleans Saints pass rush did a great job getting to Shedeur Sanders on Sunday, sacking the second-year quarterback five times while also getting three additional tackles for loss. Carl Granderson sacked Sanders twice and Chase Young sacked him once. Both players now rank in the top 3 in the NFL in sacks with 7.5 for Granderson and 8 for Young, making them arguably the best pass rushing duo in the league so far this season. Khristian Boyd also picked up his second sack of the season, and Kaden Elliss had his best game of the year with one sack and a tackle for loss. The sacks were also very timely, with two of them coming on third down and two coming in goal to go situations which helped hold the Browns to a field goal and a turnover on downs in the red zone. The Saints run game also deserves a shoutout this week, as newly returning Audric Estime ran for 72 yards and a touchdown against the team who just waived him a week prior. Estime’s 72 yards were the most by a Saint this year, a good turnaround from their last game when Tyler Shough led the team with 7 rushing yards. The Bad: Pass Blocking Despite getting to Shedeur Sanders five times, the Saints also let the Browns sack Tyler Shough five times on Sunday. Four of these sacks came on third down as well, one of which probably cost the Saints three points by turning what would’ve been a 43-yard field goal into a 52-yard field goal which was missed. Only one sack came from a defensive lineman however, as the Saints struggled to keep up with the blitzes ran by Cleveland. The Browns have been good at getting to the quarterback this year, as they came into the game averaging just under 3 sacks per game, so hopefully the Saints offensive line will improve with the return of Kelvin Banks Jr. to the lineup. The Ugly: Defensive Backs The Saints defensive backs struggled to keep up with the Browns young receivers on Sunday. They allowed receptions of 60 yards to Denzel Boston and of 64 yards to KC Concepcion which also went for a touchdown. Concepcion beat Martin Emerson Jr. deep and was able to evade both Emerson and Julian Blackmon on his way to the end zone, and Kool-Aid McKinstry got beat deep and then was unable to find an underthrown ball leading to a 60-yard catch and run by Boston. Later in overtime Justin Reid was unable to tackle Harold Fannin Jr. in the open field which led to what could’ve been the winning touchdown if the Saints didn’t stop the ensuing two-point conversion. The Saints pass defense allowed Shedeur Sanders to have arguably the best game of his career and now ranks 28th in the NFL giving up 236 yards per game.

summary: To begin the year, the fanbase was worried that the New Orleans Saints did not have a true complement on the opposite side of Chase Young to help generate pressure on opposing quarterbacks. full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - NOVEMBER 8: Carl Granderson #96 of the New Orleans Saints walks off the field following a 23-22 win against the Cleveland Browns at Caesars Superdome on November 8, 2026, in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Derick Hingle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images To begin the year, the fanbase was worried that the New Orleans Saints did not have a true complement on the opposite side of Chase Young to help generate pressure on opposing quarterbacks. Well, that question has been answered, as Carl Granderson has emerged as the missing edge rusher the Saints have needed this season. Granderson has now recorded at least 1.5 sacks in four consecutive games. He was in the backfield almost the entire game, finishing with 7 tackles, 2 sacks, 2 QB hits, and 2 tackles for loss. He now has 7.5 sacks on the season and is tied for third in the league, trailing only Chase Young, who has 8, and Will Anderson Jr., who leads the NFL with 9.5. Without the pressure and impact Granderson had on this game, the Saints may have lost. New Orleans pulled out a one-point overtime victory against a scrappy Browns team, and the defense had to make plays to keep the Saints in the game during stretches when the offense was struggling to find its rhythm. Carl Granderson is my choice for Game MVP for Week 9. Do you think the Saints have found their edge-rushing duo? And who do you think should have been the Game MVP?

title: Malik Nabers says body language claims are ‘just a lie’
summary: The New York Giants win on the road over the Philadelphia Eagles was the first in a potentially pivotal two game stretch that could all but secure them a trip to the post season. But the Giants getting their first win in Philadelphia since 2013 wasn’t the story after the game. No, the story has […]
full_text: ﻿New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers misses a touchdown catch against the Philadelphia Eagles | Getty Images The New York Giants win on the road over the Philadelphia Eagles was the first in a potentially pivotal two game stretch that could all but secure them a trip to the post season. But the Giants getting their first win in Philadelphia since 2013 wasn’t the story after the game. No, the story has somehow become the comments from Fox commenting crew Joe Davis and [former tight end] Greg Olsen regarding wide receiver Malik Nabers’ body language during the game. It started with Davis remarking that Nabers’ body language was “terrible”, and it has since spiraled into a thing . Nabers was, understandably, upset by the comments once they got back to him after the game. “I’m going to use my own voice and be able to speak up about me being a bad teammate,” he said on Tuesday. “And I felt like that was just a lie, just attacking my character as a football player and as a teammate. Like I said, I’ve never been on a team where anyone has called me a bad teammate that I know of.” In fairness to Olsen and Davis, they didn’t say that Nabers was a bad teammate during the broadcast. However, these things tend to take on a life of their own, and Nabers took issue with the comments as they were relayed to him. “I felt like after the game when I got the opportunity to hear those things, I had to speak up about that because those things (are) just not true,” he said. And as far as just the bad body language thing, everybody’s always talking about my body language. Like I’ve said, my body language is the same all the time. Whether I’m having a good game, bad game, losing, winning. You can go (to) games and you can see it for yourself if you want to go look. But as far as the bad body language and things being said that I was saying on the sideline – especially from people that’s watching the game, they don’t know what’s going on down on the field. So, you don’t know what is being said, you don’t know if I’m mad, you don’t know if I’m not. That’s just really everything on it; is my body language is the same all the time. My facial expression is the same all the time. I think a lot of people just don’t know that because they don’t know me.” “One thing about it is that I’m an ultimate competitor in whether it’s going (well) or if it’s going bad,” Nabers added. “If I make a play, my body language is I’m a mean guy, raging, slapping my helmet, screaming, never really smiling, but that’s just how I play the game of football,” he said. “I put a lot of stuff into it. I had to put a lot of great work in to get back on the field. I feel like I hold everybody to that standard to play just like that, play mean.” If there was a problem, Nabers said, it was a dissatisfaction with how the Giants were playing. In his mind, the Giants had come out of their bye week flat and were performing up to level he believes they should. “It was (the) bye week and we came off flat, we came off slow.” Nabers said. “And I was just trying to set an example of like, let’s get everybody going and my way of getting everybody is going, it’s not going (to) everybody tapping them on the leg and being nice.” “No,” he said. “it’s a game like, wake up, let’s go.” Nabers assured reporters that was was perceived as poor body language was a byproduct of his passion for the game. The Giants were struggling coming out of the bye week, and he wanted the rest of the team to match his intensity. “I’m an aggressive person when it comes to this football stuff because I’ve got a lot of passion for it,” Nabers said. “And I don’t feel like everybody knows that about me. They think my bad body language is me just not caring or I’m frustrated. No, it’s just passion for the game. I put a lot of effort into it and that can come off to anybody how they want to speak to it as far as that but like I said, it’s not hurting anyone. It’s not hurting the team. We won the game. And it got everybody able to (get) going, we scored a touchdown and everything was going great in the second half. So, I’m not (going to) speak on the bad body language because it hasn’t affected the team at all.” Now? Well Nabers is focused on the quick turnaround and facing the Washington Commanders on Thursday Night Football. But if Greg Olsen wants to reach out, he’s welcome to do so. “I think that was two days ago, three days ago and I’m focusing on the game right now. If he [Olsen] wants to reach out, he can reach out and we can have a simple conversation. But as far as – I’ve said what I said about the situation, I’m done with it.”

title: NY Giants trade deadline analysis: Nothing happened, and that’s OK
summary: The New York Giants tried to make a splash at the NFL trade deadline. They ended up not able to do anything. Running back Jonathan Taylor was, of course, the player the Giants had targeted as a difference-maker for their offense — for this season and at least a couple of years to come. The […]
full_text: John Harbaugh and the Giants will go forward without making any trades at the deadline. | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New York Giants tried to make a splash at the NFL trade deadline. They ended up not able to do anything. Running back Jonathan Taylor was, of course, the player the Giants had targeted as a difference-maker for their offense — for this season and at least a couple of years to come. The Indianapolis Colts, though, chose to set a price tag no one, including the Giants, was willing to meet. Per NFL insider Tom Pelissero : Multiple teams offered a second-round pick and more for Taylor. But the Colts wanted a blockbuster offer to even consider it. Instead, Taylor stays in Indy. Giants head coach John Harbaugh said an hour before the deadline that he would be excited to have the “right player” join the team as it tries to win its first NFC East title since 2011. “My excitement level would be based on who the player is,” Harbaugh said. “You get the right player, then you’re really excited.” Taylor could have been that guy. The price, though, was wrong. “You don’t want to make a bad deal. You make a bad deal, that doesn’t make you better. That makes you worse,” Harbaugh said. “Sometimes the best deal is a deal that you don’t make. “We’re willing to pay a price to make our team better, but it’s got to be something that really makes our team better, and it’s got to be worth it.” On Monday, I asked Harbaugh about the idea of trying not to make an emotional decision at the trade deadline with the excitement of defeating the Philadelphia Eagles and leading the division being fresh. Harbaugh said it was “very important” to take the emotion of the moment out of the decision-making process. “You want to do everything you can do to make your team as strong as you can right now, because we’re in the now, and we’re told to live in the moment, be where our feet are planted, concern ourselves with today, but that’s not at the expense of tomorrow or just prudent planning,” Harbaugh said. “I think we just have to look at each situation, and just weigh it out in terms of, okay, what’s the cost? What’s the benefit? And is it worth it? Is it going to benefit us? Is it a good thing for the Giants, and for the organization, and the team?” Taylor would have made the Giants stronger right now. The Giants, though, were correct to not overpay for a 27-year-old running back with high mileage. Just like they were correct a couple of years ago when they did not overpay in free agency for a 27-year-old running back with high mileage. In the days leading up to the deadline, we watched the Jacksonville Jaguars make multiple trades — including outrageously giving the Philadelphia Eagles first- and second-round picks for defensive tackle Jordan Davis. We saw the Minnesota Vikings trade for quarterback Kirk Cousins. We saw the Buffalo Bills, San Francisco 49ers, and Kansas City Chiefs make “now” trades. All of those teams have designs on winning a Super Bowl this season. The Giants? They are not there yet. Winning the NFC East would be a massive accomplishment. Remember, they won seven games combined the last two seasons. It would be a tremendous step in the right direction for a proud franchise that has been down for most of the last 15 years. I went on record a few days ago saying that I thought the Giants should make another run at Taylor, but that the price couldn’t be more than the second-round pick plus that they had already offered. Not giving away their first-round pick was the proper decision. In Harbaugh’s words, the prudent one. The Tennessee Titans did not want to trade running back Tony Pollard. He is a nice player, but Skattebo and Tyrone Tracy are nice players, too. The Giants could have used defensive tackle help. They were never getting Jeffery Simmons, and they weren’t foolish enough to give up a first-round pick for Davis. The Colts apparently wanted a fourth-round pick for Grover Stewart. The Giants didn’t have one to give. They do have Malachi Fields. They didn’t have a fifth-round pick. They do have J.J. McCarthy. Harbaugh had warned on Sunday that the Giants would protect their future. “We’re not just going to go for a short term fix at an exorbitant cost,” he said. “We’re not going to do that. That’s not where we’re at.” Where they are at is leading the NFC East by 2.5 games. They have a 68.9% chance of winning the division , moves or no moves. Getting Taylor, or another big-time difference-maker at the deadline would have been nice. In the end, though, I think fans should be happy that Harbaugh and GM Joe Schoen kep their wits about them and protected the future. The deadline end up to be boring for the Giants. Disappointing even, if you want to call it that. But, the Giants acted properly rather than desperately. That was a victory of sorts by itself.

title: How the NY Giants Dennard Wilson, Arvell Reese destroyed the Eagles’ passing attack
summary: The New York Giants have one of the NFL’s most promising young coaches in Dennard Wilson, who is finding ways to maximize the immense young talent on the roster. Rookie linebacker Arvell Reese credited the coaching staff’s strategic use of him as a key factor in his success. Reese had 1.5 sacks and six pressures […]
full_text: Arvell Reese | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New York Giants have one of the NFL’s most promising young coaches in Dennard Wilson, who is finding ways to maximize the immense young talent on the roster. Rookie linebacker Arvell Reese credited the coaching staff’s strategic use of him as a key factor in his success. Reese had 1.5 sacks and six pressures heading into the Giants’ Week 9 matchup against the Philadelphia Eagles. The Giants traded Dexter Lawrence during the offseason, leaving a significant void in their ability to generate interior pressure. Lawrence had been a consistent force disrupting quarterbacks from the inside, but Wilson has found another way to manufacture pressure through creative blitz packages that attack the interior. He recognizes Reese’s ability as a pass rusher and the mismatch he creates when matched up against running backs in pass protection. Dennard Wilson has done an elite job scheming to the strengths of rookie LB Arvell Reese. Stack LBs w/ 5 man pressure…send Harris (1T) wide & Pinnock through the B to expand the OGs and isolate Reese vs. RB in protection. Reese is a weapon Wilson knows how to use best. pic.twitter.com/VG1fJjOryB — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) November 9, 2026 New York deployed a variety of pressure looks aimed at the center and guards, with defensive linemen widening their rush paths to manipulate the protection. Players like Kayvon Thibodeaux (5) would feign an outside rush, forcing offensive linemen to account for them as potential threats. This approach occupies blockers and creates advantageous one-on-one matchups elsewhere along the line — opportunities that a versatile talent like Arvell Reese can exploit. The hit heard around the world Charlie Jones fumbled a punt giving the Eagles the ball in Giants’ territory with all the momentum in the world; a situation that would have crippled past Giants’ teams. However, New York forced a third-and-5 pass attempt where Joe Milton was hit hard Reese: Arvell Reese knocked Joe Milton into next week pic.twitter.com/bfnKLaS0dV — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) November 9, 2026 New York schemed three over two to the offensive left side ( where Reese was) ; Dawuane Smoot (96) aligned as a 4i-shade, with Thibodeaux wide of the tackle and Reese wide of Thibodeaux. Micah McFadden (41) sugared the A-Gap, forcing center attention, with Darius Alexander as a three-technique (91), Abdul Carter (3) as a five-technique, and Dru Phillips (22) wide of Carter. The loaded line of scrimmage led to Saquon Barkley (26) accounting for McFadden and the three other rushers to the offensive right – and NO ONE accounted for Reese the left, including Milton. Both Smoot and Alexander dropped off into coverage, with Thibodeaux acting effectively as a spy once his initial rush was stopped and the four-man rush got home for an unblocked sack-forced fumble. Here’s another video of the hit: This sack by Arvell Reese was the fastest (2.29 seconds) in the NFL since week 7 of last season, according to @NextGenStats Reese is the only NFL player with 65+ tackles, 8+ TFL, 1+ INT so far in 2026. pic.twitter.com/uaNi5EmRzC — Dane Brugler (@dpbrugler) November 9, 2026 Reese’s second sack via GIPHY Reese had another third-down sack, this time on third-and-10. Wilson overloaded the offensive right side with four players on the line of scrimmage: Thibodeaux, Smoot, Alexander, and Tae Banks (2); Wilson aggressively aligns the corners in press coverage versus condensed fronts to gain a numbers advantage in the pass rush — Wilson isn’t shy about sending the cornerback to creatively cover the receiver. Reese is stacked behind Alexander, and he slants opposite to the protection slide toward McFadden and Carter, who both have one-on-one matchups due to the pressure-look. Elijah Mitchell (39) did an excellent job picking up McFadden, and Reese was stopped by the guard, so he slid off the rush and eyed Milton, who attempted to run into green grass, but instead found the waiting arms of an elite Ohio State rookie linebacker. Reese’s third sack via GIPHY Reese’s third sack came on third-and-10 with 7:22 left in the fourth quarter. Reese was aligned off the line of scrimmage in a 4i-shade with Thibodeaux to his right, wide of the tackle. Alexander was over the center, which isolated Reese against the guard, Landon Dickerson (69). New York ran a game with Reese penetrating the B-Gap for Thibodeaux to undercut and loop into the A-Gap, while another twist happened with Alexander and Carter. Final thoughts Wilson is on a tear. He’s generating pressure in a variety of different ways with a lot of exotic coverage looks on the back-end. Wilson uses disguise on a loaded line of scrimmage, while dropping his short-zone coverages off the line of scrimmage after declaring a rush, which effectively wastes blockers and isolates players like Reese and Abdul Carter into valuable one-on-one matchups. Not only do the Giants have immensely talented young defensive players, but the coach understands how to best maximize the talent. Arvell Reese is now the favorite to win defensive rookie of the year, but conversations about defensive player of the year are starting to happen. With performances like Week 9, it’s not crazy to mention his name in that conversation.
