title: Seven things Solak thinks for NFL Week 10: Jaguars trades, All-Pro picks, more
summary: Get ready for Week 10 with takes on the Jaguars winning the AFC, Shedeur Sanders not earning a starting role, Fred Warner being the best player in football and more.
full_text:
Are you excited for NFL Week 10 ? With nine weeks in the history books and nine more weeks to go, I can't remember a season with as dense a top tier of NFL contenders. Nobody feels immortal, but many teams feel mighty. We're gonna learn a lot in Week 10 -- the Patriots against the Lions in Munich, the Vikings in Green Bay for a critical divisional rematch, and the Steelers at the Bengals on Sunday night -- and a lot more in the weeks to come. November should be fun.

 Every Tuesday of the NFL season , I'll turn the page from the previous week to the upcoming one with seven things I think. These aren't full-scale predictions. They aren't concrete takeaways from the past week of NFL action, either; those are fired off Sunday or Monday. Instead, these are the uncertain topics. They are things that might be true, but it'll probably take the next few games to find out. And at the bottom, you'll find a few extra half-thoughts ... just those little inklings I'm unable to shake.

 
 Subscribe: 'ESPN's Leaguewide' 

 
 This week, I'll start by lauding the Jaguars for going all-in on the trade deadline Monday, play some deadline bingo and then cast my votes for a midseason All-Pro team.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Jaguars are AFC favorites?   
 Quiet trade deadline on the horizon? 
 Who makes the midseason All-Pro team? 
 Sanders isn't good enough to unseat Watson? 
 Could Lock be a bridge QB in 2027? 
 Warner is the best football player? 
 Some extra inklings 

 
 

 

 I think ... the Jaguars are going to win the AFC (and maybe more) 
 They certainly think so, too!

 Monday was Jaguars day in the NFL, as second-year general manager James Gladstone made three trades during the day. He sent a 2027 second-rounder and 2028 fifth-rounder to Atlanta for safety Jessie Bates III . Then, he sent a 2028 sixth-rounder to the Saints for nose tackle Davon Godchaux . These two trades addressed Jacksonville's two biggest sudden needs after the season-ending injuries to safety Eric Murray and nose tackle DaVon Hamilton .

 

 But then, the stunner: The Jaguars sent their 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick to the Eagles for defensive tackle Jordan Davis , a premier run stuffer whom the Eagles had given a three-year, $78 million extension in March.

 It doesn't take a degree in trade deadline analysis to figure out that the 6-2 Jaguars, who traded away five picks, three of which were top-64 selections, are going for broke with a team they believe is on the inside track for the Super Bowl. These three players all serve critical roles in that effort. Let's talk about all three, starting with the most important.

 Godchaux is a -- nah. Just messing.

 Davis is a tricky player to figure out. He broke out in 2025 -- Year 4 of his NFL career -- with a career-best 16.5% run stop rate, good for fourth best among all defensive tackles. His run stop EPA (total value he generated on all of his run stops) was also fourth in the league. He ranked alongside Cameron Heyward , Quinnen Williams , Leonard Williams and Jeffery Simmons . 

 Year 3 or Year 4 breakouts for defensive tackles -- especially heavier tackles who really need to manage their weight and conditioning -- are more common than you'd think. Vita Vea made his first Pro Bowl in Year 4 and had his best run stop rate and run stop EPA of his career in that season. Dexter Lawrence II was a good run stuffer early but popped as a pass rusher in Year 4, as his pressure rate in that season remains his career-best mark.

 Davis entered 2025 with a lighter frame and tremendous conditioning. This season, Davis has seemed slower and more prone to sitting on blocks. His effort has waned at times. He could be in worse shape. He could also be disengaged from a bad team and bad defense overall.

 The Jaguars are betting that he'll play better on their competitive roster -- perhaps something closer to his 2025 form. They need him to, as he has huge shoes to fill. Through the first seven weeks of the season, the Jaguars' defense was the league's best against running back carries, ranking first in yards allowed per carry, first in yards allowed per game, first in success rate, second in EPA per carry allowed and first in opponent first-down rate. Hamilton was not the only contributor to that effort (edges Travon Walker and Josh Hines-Allen help, too), but he was key. The Jaguars want to be a light box defense -- six or fewer defenders in the box -- (35.6% light boxes through Week 7, 10th-highest rate) and need defensive linemen who can take more than one opposing player in the run fit. Hamilton was that player for them on the interior ... a space eater.

 

 Hamilton went down with a season-ending injury early in Week 8, and the potential decline in the Jaguars' run defense became a weakness worth monitoring. And the trade for Davis makes it clear that the Jaguars believe their defensive structure doesn't work without that scale-tipping player at nose tackle. When Hamilton was healthy, the Jaguars were allowing 3.8 yards per play with him on the field and 6.9 yards per play with him off the field, per NFL Next Gen Stats. That role cannot be platooned.

 Hamilton wasn't much of a pass rusher for the Jaguars, and Davis doesn't need to be, either. The Jags are one of the most aggressive teams in the league for mug fronts (defenders filling gaps near the line of scrimmage), stunts and twists, and fire zone blitzes. Remember, defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile was Brian Flores' linebackers coach for three seasons in Miami before he spent one year under Vic Fangio, who coached Davis in Philadelphia. (That shared year of language should help ease Davis' on-ramp into the new defense.)

 Though Campanile's blitz rate (30.9%) doesn't look particularly Floresian, he spins many of the same dials. The Jaguars are seventh in team pressure rate and first in time to pressure (Vikings are first and fifth, respectively) thanks to how many free rushers they manufacture in their blitzes and simulated pressures. Minnesota is first in quick pressure rate; Jacksonville is third. The Jaguars are second in total unblocked pressures; the Vikings are fourth.

 Flores uses these wild blitz looks on all three downs, and Campanile deploys them on long-and-late downs. Davis' value will be in creating run stuffs and manufacturing more second-and-longs and third-and-longs. He'll come off the field for these heavy-blitz looks and never have a high pass rush win rate accordingly, but his wins on early downs create these opportunities. The same can be said for Godchaux as Davis' backup.

 Bates, meanwhile, will be on the field for all of those wacky third downs, and he will feast on them. He is one of the smartest players on the field at any given time, quarterbacks included. The 29-year-old is not as fast as he once was, but his play recognition and ball skills still allow him to make high-impact plays on the football (three forced fumbles, four passes defensed). The Jaguars manufacture plays on the ball already; they're second in the league in defensive turnover EPA since the start of this season and first since the start of last season. Bates is another player who is excellent at addressing the football.

 So why make the move? Well, the Jaguars still needed better coverage presence in the last level of the defense. All of their defensive metrics are healthy -- third in EPA per drive, second in success rate, second in points allowed per drive -- save for one: explosive pass rate. They allowed an explosive pass on 14.4% of dropbacks, the sixth-highest rate. If Bates' center-field presence knocks that number down to league average, the Jaguars' defense will be difficult to expose.

 

 Bates is also a great tackler, which is critical in this system. Thanks to all the coverage rotations, mugged looks and sudden droppers, the ball comes out fast against Jacksonville. Opposing quarterbacks have a 2.73-second time to throw (fourth fastest) against the Jags' defense, and…

title: Cowboys rave about Quinnen Williams a year after trade deadline deal
summary: Voted a captain by his teammates, Williams is making a difference in Dallas on and off the field.
full_text:
FRISCO, Texas -- In his past few meetings with the media, Dallas Cowboys defensive tackle Quinnen Williams has come up with a couple of phrases for when he does not want to address a certain subject or does not know enough about one to comment.

 One common refrain has been: "I've got to think about that."

 Another has been: "I'm going to keep that to myself."

 Recently, he said he was not playing in a dominant manner, that he needed to fine tune and fix some things.

 

 "I know exactly how it's supposed to look, how it's supposed to feel when it gets there," Williams said. "Right now, I can just focus on getting better, the things I did wrong, the things I need to do better and keep going in the right direction. When that game comes, when that game hits, I can build off that with momentum."

 What exactly is missing?

 "I'm going to keep that to myself," he said.

 Whatever is missing might be the most minute details that only he and limited number of players in his stratosphere can understand. Williams called his 2022 season with the New York Jets his standard when he had 12 sacks, 12 tackles for loss (TFL), 28 quarterback pressures, four pass breakups, two forced fumbles and a fumble recovery.

 Through nine games this season, Williams leads the Cowboys in sacks (five), tackles for loss (14) and forced fumbles (two). He is second in quarterback hurries (29).

 "If there's a better interior defensive lineman than him in the league, I haven't been around one in a long time," coach Brian Schottenheimer said. "He's just dominated the way he can change the game."

 

 He has recorded at least two tackles for loss in each of his past four games. Only linebacker  DeMarcus Ware (five) has a longer streak by a Cowboy since TFLs began being tracked in 1999. His 14 TFLs are the most by a Cowboys defensive tackle in the first nine games of a season. Only Ware had more (18 in 2011).

 He had three tackles for loss in last week's 27-23 win against the Indianapolis Colts . His biggest came on the Colts' second-to-last drive, when Indianapolis could have run down the clock to make the Cowboys' comeback more difficult, as he stopped  Jonathan Taylor for a 1-yard loss.

 Earlier in the fourth quarter, Williams stopped Taylor for a 2-yard loss and forced a fumble that linebacker Shemar James recovered.

 "I told him during the game, in the midst of the fire, 'I love playing by you,'" James said. "He's the guy that makes plays. He's the guy that's vocal, that runs his room, controls his room. And ultimately he's just a great leader and a great player."

 It's been a little more than a calendar year since the Cowboys acquired Williams from the Jets for a 2026 second-round pick and 2027 first-rounder. In 16 games with Dallas, he has been credited with 56 tackles, 6.5 sacks, 62 quarterback hurries, two forced fumbles, two pass breakups and an interception.

 

 "I think he's fully within that flow really since Week 3," defensive coordinator Christian Parker said recently. "And he wasn't playing bad the first two weeks, just wasn't the dynamic impact that we all know he's capable of.

 "I think that he's just been comfortable with himself, No. 1, and comfortable with the people around him. And he knows just to cut it loose and go play and we'll make the corrections. I tell him all the time, 'Your mistakes belong to me,' so as long as you play fast and aggressive, we can fix everything else."

 Kenny Clark , Williams' defensive tackle running mate the past 16 games, is a three-time Pro Bowler himself and knows what it is supposed to look like.

 "Just his ability to play fast," Clark said. "Actually, I was watching the film, he's just dominant. He's just dominant in there. He does a great job of finishing, whether it's him getting TFLs or getting tackles on the running backs or finishing his rushes, getting sacks and stuff like that. He does a great job of finishing. He's a complete player. It's not much that he can't do."

 Off the field, Williams' voice has become one of the most important in the locker room. Before the win against the Philadelphia Eagles , Williams gave a pregame talk. He was not interested in divulging what he said or why he said it.

 "I'm going to keep that to myself," he said.

 He was voted a captain by his teammates, along with Clark, quarterback  Dak Prescott and kicker  Brandon Aubrey . He is on the player council that reports to Schottenheimer when issues arise. During the struggles of the Cowboys' defense, he has repeatedly mentioned there are more things he can do, taking accountability for the group.

 

 Inside The Star, the Cowboys' practice facility, his locker is next to Prescott's.

 "There's a guy who loves this game, loves his teammates," Prescott said. "I'm fortunate to be a locker over from him to have conversations throughout the week about leadership and how to get his side going versus our side going and what we need to do for the team.

 "One of my favorite teammates all time and super thankful for that guy, for the way that he's wired. He plays this game the right way. He loves this game the right way and it shows. It shows every time. Every snap that he plays, he puts it out there."

 After he signed his three-year, $105 million extension in training camp, Williams spoke about his desire to make the playoffs for the first time in his career and win a Super Bowl. At 4-5, the Cowboys are still in the NFC East race , but that might be their only path to the postseason.

 If the Cowboys are to truly contend, they need Williams to continue to chase his standard.

 Williams said he is heading in "the right direction on what I want to do, what I want to be, who I want to be, how I want to affect the game. I got to continue to execute, continue to do the things I know I can do to help this defense turn around and help this team win football games."

title: From 2-7 to 6-2: Josh Downs reacts to Chiefs trade with Vince Carter GIF
summary: A moment from Vince Carter's retirement ceremony helped Downs sum up his feelings about joining Kansas City.
full_text:
Josh Downs needed only one GIF to show how he felt about going from the 2-7 Indianapolis Colts to the 6-2 Kansas City Chiefs .

 

 After Tuesday's trade , the wide receiver posted a popular clip of Vince Carter overcome with emotion during his Toronto Raptors jersey retirement ceremony. Often used to celebrate good news, the GIF presumably represented Downs' feelings about his new destination.

 The moment dates to Nov. 2, 2024, when Carter became the first player to have his jersey retired by the Raptors . His emotional reaction as Toronto honored his No. 15 has since taken on a life of its own online.

 Downs' post also caught the attention of his new quarterback, Patrick Mahomes , who reposted it with a clock emoji.

 

 Downs, who had requested a trade, heads to Kansas City with a 2027 seventh-round pick in exchange for fourth- and fifth-round selections. He brings 33 catches for 354 yards and a touchdown this season to a Chiefs receiver group dealing with injuries to Tyquan Thornton and Xavier Worthy .

 The GIF wasn't Downs' only message Tuesday. He also thanked the team that drafted him in the third round in 2023.

 "I am beyond grateful and blessed for my time in Indy. Nothing but love For the Shoe," he wrote on X.

title: Questions on 2026 NFL trade deadline deals: Does Kirk Cousins lift the Vikings?
summary: Let's make sense of Kirk Cousins to the Vikings, Josh Downs to the Chiefs, the Jaguars getting aggressive, a wild Bengals comp-pick mixup and four teams' deadline silence.
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline has come and gone. For all the big names rumored to be in the mix Tuesday afternoon, the most significant trade involved Titans safety Amani Hooker , who was dealt to the Bills with a fifth-round pick for a second-round selection. The Vikings reunited with quarterback  Kirk Cousins for a third-round selection, but the biggest moves ended up taking place Monday, when the Jaguars sent out a first-round pick and two second-round selections to land Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates III .

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 With the final trades of the 2026 season in the books, what we saw over the past 24 hours left me with more questions than answers. And so with that in mind, I set out to try to answer those questions.

 I'll get to the Cousins deal, a trade that was ruined by the internet and the teams that missed an opportunity to make a deal, but I have to start this in Florida, where a Jags regime that has been very happy to bet on themselves doubled down.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Did the Jaguars give up too much? 
 Can Cousins elevate the Vikings enough? 
 How happened with the Bengals? 
 What does Downs mean for the Chiefs? 
 Why weren't there more trades? 
 Which teams missed out? 

 
 

 

 Did the Jaguars give up too much to address two injuries on their roster? 
 The most fascinating team at the deadline did its work Monday with a series of stunning trades. The impetus for those moves, seemingly, goes back to a pair of relatively under-the-radar injuries  in the Week 8 win over the Colts . During that game, defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton tore his quadriceps muscle, and safety Eric Murray injured his elbow. Both are expected to sit out the rest of the season.

 Hamilton and Murray aren't bad players -- Hamilton was having his best season as a pro -- but they're not the sort of load-bearing, cornerstone contributors who would lead a front office to panic that the defense will collapse without them. It was surprising, then, that the Jaguars decided to fill those holes by sacrificing a significant portion of their high-end draft capital over the next three years.

 

 First, general manager James Gladstone & Co. addressed safety by trading second- and fifth-round picks to the Falcons for veteran  Jessie Bates III , whose contract expires at the end of the season. Trading a sixth-round pick to the Saints for Davon Godchaux seemed like a logical addition in terms of adding a rotational defensive tackle, but the Jaguars went over the top Monday evening, sending first- and second-round picks to the Eagles for fellow defensive tackle  Jordan Davis . Suddenly, the Jags look as if they're all-in, and it's to fill holes that didn't really seem as if they were huge liabilities.

 Let's start by talking about the players. It's easy to understand why Jacksonville would be excited. Bates is a leader and a playmaker on the back end, where his instincts and experience help get him into throwing lanes and in position to break up passes. He hasn't missed a start since leaving for Atlanta in 2023, which helps mitigate some of the concerns about his advancing age, given that Bates turns 30 in February.

 The league is generally very anxious about targeting safeties with significant contracts as they hit 30 given the sheer need to cover ground while playing as a single-high or two-deep free safety. I'm not concerned about that with Bates at the moment. He has covered an average of 16.7 yards per play so far this season, per NFL Next Gen Stats, in line with what he did in 2023 (16.8), 2024 (17.0) and 2025 (16.7), when the Falcons aligned him near the line of scrimmage more often than they had in past years.

 I'm not sure there's evidence that his ability to access top speeds has fallen dramatically. According to Next Gen Stats, he has topped 19 mph three times through nine weeks, which is in line with his averages through the first half of the season in each of the three previous years with the Falcons. One measure I use as an estimate is a player's average 90th percentile maximum speed, which tries to measure the speed each player is likely to get to on the vast majority of their snaps. Bates' 2026 figure there (15.6 mph) is higher than it was in any of his previous seasons with Atlanta.

 Godchaux is a reasonable nose tackle, but he now projects to be in a backup role behind Davis, who was added to be an essential player for the Jaguars up front. The Eagles moved up ahead of the Ravens in 2022 to take Davis with the 13th pick in the draft, forcing Baltimore to "settle" for safety  Kyle Hamilton with the 14th selection. The expectation was that Davis would have a floor as an excellent run stopper, while his high-end athleticism raised hopes that he would end up developing into a significant pass-rushing threat on the interior with more experience and NFL coaching.

 That hasn't really come together. Despite playing next to Fletcher Cox, Jalen Carter  and Milton Williams at different times during his run in Philadelphia, Davis hasn't been able to create steady pass pressure. Davis has 9.5 sacks and 15 knockdowns over 4½ years as a pro. And those really haven't typically been a direct product of Davis creating opportunities, such as last week's sack against the Giants , where Davis twisted with Carter and the latter came free, only for  J.J. McCarthy  to duck under the initial sack of Carter and into the arms of Davis.

 

 Since entering the starting lineup for good in 2023, Davis has generated pressures on 5.6% of his pass-rush snaps and 1.2% of his quick pressures. Among defensive tackles with 700 pass-rush opportunities or more over that timeframe, Davis ranks 63rd out of 71 qualifiers in pressure rate and 60th in quick pressure rate. Godchaux, for what it's worth, ranks 71st in both categories.

 Davis is a good two-down nose tackle. I'm assuming the Jags think he still has another gear to hit. For one, they can follow in the footsteps of what the Eagles did when they got A.J. Brown and simply play him more often. Davis hasn't sat out a regular-season start since the start of 2023, but with the Eagles rotating Davis alongside Moro Ojomo , Williams and others over the years, he has played about only 48% of Philly's defensive snaps in that span, dropping just below 25% on third downs.

 Getting Davis on the field on third downs will simply get him in the lineup against pass plays more often, which would give him more opportunities to get after the quarterback. The Jaguars also might greenlight Davis to be more aggressive getting into the backfield with opportunities to one-gap as opposed to playing the gap-and-a-half style that Vic Fangio employs with his defensive tackles. I'd be surprised if Davis became a great pass rusher after not showing it for four-plus years, but I wouldn't be shocked if his pass-rush production improved with the move to Jacksonville.

 That's the good news. The prices the Jags paid to get those guys? That's the bad news. These were trades in which the guys on the other side of the phone had to ask twice to make sure that the rounds they were hearing were correct. The Eagles just signed Davis to a contract extension in March and paid him an $18.8 million bonus in the process; I suspect they asked  LeBron James  if they could borrow his helicopter to get Davis to the airport before the Jaguars changed their mind.

 Bates is a pure half-season player since his contract expires at the end of the season. The Jaguars could re-sign him, of course, but they could also have gone after him (or a replacement) in free agency next offseason, and signing him would be locking the team in for what are likely to be Bates' decline years. As my colleague Seth Walder noted , the Jags are far more likely to recoup a compensatory pick for Bates than the Falcons, but I'm at least a little skeptical that it'll be a significant selection. The last time a safety on the wrong side of 30 even qualified for anything higher than a sixth-round…

title: Chiefs add WR Josh Downs at NFL trade deadline
summary: Nate Taylor discusses what adding WR Josh Downs could mean for Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs.

title: How Josh Downs fits with Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs' offense
summary: Former Colts WR Downs brings speed, route running and big-play ability to a Kansas City offense in need of all three.
full_text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- Josh Downs celebrated almost immediately.

 Using his X account Tuesday afternoon, Downs, the Kansas City Chiefs ' newest receiver, posted the popular GIF of Vince Carter, the NBA legend overwhelmed with emotion when the Toronto Raptors retired his jersey. Downs wanted to express his joy for a variety of reasons -- his newest quarterback is Patrick Mahomes , his newest coach is Andy Reid and he is the newest member of the Chiefs, one of the top contenders in the AFC.

 The Chiefs bolstered their passing attack just before the NFL's trade deadline by acquiring Downs, a fourth-year player, from the Indianapolis Colts . The deal included the Chiefs sending 2027 fourth- and fifth-round picks to the Colts for Downs and a 2027 seventh-round pick.

 Mahomes celebrated the move, orchestrated by general manager Brett Veach, by using his X account to post the alarm clock emoji, indicating he is ready to start working with Downs to improve the Chiefs' offense.

 Last month, Downs, who will be a free agent after this season, requested to be traded from the Colts. One reason, according to sources with knowledge of his thinking, was Downs knowing he had the potential to play alongside Mahomes and the rest of the Chiefs' stars on offense, including running back Kenneth Walker III , tight end Travis Kelce and fellow receiver Rashee Rice .

 

 The week before the Chiefs' 35-12 defeat of the New York Jets on Sunday, the team had offered a fourth-round pick to the Colts for Downs, according to a source with knowledge of the negotiation. The Colts, who had already traded left guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner , were hoping to persuade a team to offer a third-round pick for Downs. The Chiefs' willingness to swap 2027 Day 3 picks with the Colts was the final piece for both teams to agree to consummate the trade.

 "I am beyond grateful and blessed for my time in Indy," Downs wrote on his X account Tuesday. "Nothing but love For the Shoe."

 In nine games this season, Downs recorded 33 receptions on 56 targets for 354 yards and one touchdown.

 Improving the receiving position was the Chiefs' biggest need ahead of the trade deadline. One reason the Chiefs needed to add another receiver was a lack of production at the position. Heading into Week 10, Downs' production this season exceeds that of any receiver on Kansas City's roster; Rice leads the Chiefs' wideouts with 25 receptions on 31 targets for 292 yards.

 The lack of production from the Chiefs' collection of receivers -- Rice, Xavier Worthy , rookie Cyrus Allen , Andrew Armstrong and Jalen Royals -- over the past four games made it difficult for Mahomes to have success when passing downfield. Since a Week 4 win over the Las Vegas Raiders , Mahomes hasn't completed a pass of over 20 air yards. That stat coincides with the loss of the Chiefs' best deep threat to that point, receiver Tyquan Thornton , who suffered a dislocated left ankle in the game against Las Vegas.

 Downs should be beneficial to Mahomes because of his combination of quickness at the line of scrimmage, speed in the open field and ability to get open with crisp route running, especially from the slot. The Chiefs experienced Downs' talents in their Week 2 win over the Colts, when he, mostly running his routes from the slot, led Indy with seven receptions on nine targets for 72 yards.

 

 "[Against] man coverage, he's going to win," ESPN analyst Dan Orlovsky, a former NFL quarterback, said Tuesday on "NFL Live" in reaction to the trade. "[In] Week 2, he was unguardable. This fills a need, but also it's, 'Who are we going to have to beat?' If you're going to play Cincinnati, they like to play a decent amount of man coverage. Jacksonville, they'll play a lot of match coverage [with man principles]. Buffalo has played more man coverage recently.

 "They needed another receiver that could become reliable."

 Downs' play has been inconsistent since the start of October. He has produced 168 receiving yards and one touchdown over the past six games. In his final game with Indy, a loss to the Dallas Cowboys , Downs had two critical dropped passes.

 The Chiefs also shouldn't expect Downs to be a receiver who can dominate games and shoulder a lot of targets, like many No. 1 receivers across the league. In his career, Downs has generated 100 or more receiving yards just twice.

 

 The Chiefs, though, are optimistic that Downs will be able to complement Kelce, Rice and Walker, who has already recorded a career-high four receiving touchdowns this season.

 Downs' speed and his history for generating long receptions should allow Mahomes to have a viable option when opposing defenses put eight defenders in the box to account for Walker's rushing threat. In his career, Downs has receptions of 59, 69, 34 and 42 yards. Any of those gains would be a season long for every Chief except Worthy, whose longest reception is 41 yards. Downs' five receptions of 20 yards or more are also more than any Chiefs wideout.

 Mahomes didn't have similar big-play ability last week against the Jets. In that game, Mahomes averaged just 2.8 air yards per attempt, his second lowest in a game in his career, according to NFL Next Gen Stats, despite finishing with 242 yards and two touchdowns. The Chiefs' fastest receiver that day, Worthy, suffered a left hamstring injury late in the fourth quarter, which could force him to miss the team's game against the Atlanta Falcons on Sunday.

 Though he'll have only three practices with his new teammates before facing the Falcons, Downs is expected to play a role in the Chiefs' game plan. Starting Sunday, Downs will have nine games left in the regular season to see how quickly he and Mahomes can build their chemistry and how much they can help the team put more points on the scoreboard.

 "They've got to be smart and be able to pick [the playbook] up quickly," Reid said two weeks ago of the Chiefs potentially adding a receiver. "I've had players that have done that. But I would tell you there better be some form of aptitude there, capacity, because you're jumping in the middle of things."

title: Patrick and Brittany Mahomes announce baby No. 4 on NFL trade deadline day

full_text:
Trade deadline day in the NFL brought additions on and off the field for Patrick Mahomes .

 

 The Kansas City Chiefs quarterback and his wife, Brittany, announced Tuesday in a joint Instagram post that they are expecting their fourth child. The couple shared beachside family photos featuring their three children in the announcement.

 "Another blessing from God ... & then there were 6," they wrote with accompanying emojis.

 

 The announcement means another sibling for daughters Sterling Skye, 5, and Golden Raye, 1, and son Patrick "Bronze" Lavon Mahomes III, 3. Patrick and Brittany were high school sweethearts in Texas before getting married in Hawaii in March 2022 .

 The family announcement capped a busy day for Mahomes, who also welcomed a new teammate in Kansas City . Earlier Tuesday, the Chiefs acquired wide receiver Josh Downs and a 2027 seventh-round pick from the Indianapolis Colts for fourth- and fifth-round selections.

title: What the Kirk Cousins trade means for the Vikings and the Raiders
summary: We answered big questions surrounding the trade of quarterback Kirk Cousins from the Raiders to the Vikings.
full_text:
Kirk Cousins played what appeared to be his final game for the Minnesota Vikings on Oct. 29, 2023. 

 On that afternoon at Lambeau Field, Cousins had thrown for 274 yards and two touchdowns when he tore his right Achilles tendon and was lost for the season. That moment set off a three-year odyssey that improbably ended the way it began. 

 Cousins returned Tuesday to the Vikings, via a trade that sent their 2027 third-round draft pick to the Las Vegas Raiders , and could start Sunday's game against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field ( 1 p.m. ET, Fox ). Since then, the Vikings have tried eight different starting quarterbacks and made a total of 14 different in-season quarterback changes. 

 The most recent came Monday night at U.S. Bank Stadium, where Carson Wentz -- starting in place of the injured Kyler Murray -- produced the Vikings' worst game by a starting quarterback since 2006. The Vikings have lost consecutive games after a 6-0 start, and their decision-makers did not want to waste what has been an elite-level defense and special teams performance this season with poor quarterback play. 

 In Las Vegas, the door is now wide open for Fernando Mendoza , the No. 1 pick of the 2026 NFL draft, to step into his role as the long-term franchise quarterback.

 ESPN Vikings reporter Kevin Seifert, Raiders reporter Ryan McFadden, national reporter Jeremy Fowler and fantasy's Michael F. Florio take a closer look at the questions and issues involved.

 

 

 What's a realistic expectation for the Vikings' offense with Cousins at QB? 
 The offense under coach Kevin O'Connell has been tough for quarterbacks of all experience levels to master, and Cousins talked often in 2022 about his struggles to feel comfortable in it. But by the middle of the 2023 season, Cousins was playing better than he ever had in a Minnesota uniform. He led the NFL with 18 touchdown passes over eight games and had a 64 QBR. All of which goes to say that if he can pick up where he left off, the Vikings could soon resurrect their dormant passing offense. But it's only natural to expect Cousins to need some time to adjust after three years away, and it also might be a generous assumption that the quarterback position is the only cause of their issues this season. It's only fair to say that playcalling, pass protection and run game efficiency have also contributed. -- Seifert 

 

 If Cousins isn't able to ignite the Vikings' offense, what does it mean for Kevin O'Connell's future in Minnesota? 
 If that is the outcome, and the Vikings miss the playoffs following a 6-0 start, there won't be many people left to blame. Owners Zygi and Mark Wilf have already fired general manager Kwesi Adofo-Mensah, whom they hired alongside O'Connell in 2022. O'Connell reports directly to the Wilfs, not to new general manager Nolan Teasley, but the Vikings' offensive collapse now goes all the way back to the start of the 2025 season. If he can't make it work with Cousins -- and to be fair it's far from easy to integrate a new starting quarterback in midseason -- then O'Connell's future will at the very least come under heavy offseason scrutiny. The Wilfs love the locker room culture O'Connell has created with his empathetic personality, but his specialty on the field -- offense, in particular the passing game -- has been substandard for an extended period of time. -- Seifert 

 
 

 Is Fernando Mendoza now the Raiders' starting quarterback? What should we expect from him? 
 GM John Spytek officially named Mendoza the Raiders' starting quarterback on Tuesday. Despite Mendoza not playing in games, the Raiders have been pleased with the progress that he made behind the scenes. Quarterbacks coach Mike Sullivan has praised Mendoza for developing stronger command of the offense. He noticed Mendoza's command and how the game slowed down for him during his debut against the Patriots in Week 5.

 Sure, Mendoza doesn't have the experience that Cousins possessed (nor does  Aidan O'Connell ). But the reigning Heisman Trophy winner has a stronger arm than Cousins. On top of that, Mendoza has better mobility, which will be helpful on bootleg plays. Mendoza will not be perfect and patience will be required, especially in the first few weeks as the starter. It does help that he has the best tight ends room in the league with Brock Bowers and Michael Mayer , and the offensive line has been fairly solid in pass protection. Mendoza taking over will be a perfect time for the Raiders to fix their running game to better support the rookie. -- McFadden 

 

 What does this trade mean for the fantasy value of players in Minnesota and Las Vegas? 
 The biggest winner of this trade is wide receiver  Justin Jefferson . He has averaged a career-low 56.1 receiving yards per game this season, after averaging 61.6 per game in 2025. In his four seasons with Cousins, Jefferson averaged 98 yards per game and had a 17-game pace of 1,671 yards and 8.5 touchdowns. He remains a must-start fantasy option and could once again reach elite status with Cousins, especially since the Vikings have the seventh-best remaining WR schedule.

 Cousins had been enjoying a resurgence in Vegas this season, averaging 19.1 fantasy points per game and is currently the QB5 in total points. Perhaps there is a ramp-up period as he adjusts to a new team, but Cousins knows O'Connell's system well. Expect Cousins to hold similar fantasy value with the Vikings as he did with the Raiders, in the low-end QB1/high-end QB2 range.

 As for the Raiders, while Mendoza is very talented, a change to a rookie QB always adds some volatility. He is worth adding off the waiver wire for QB-needy teams, as there will be games when Mendoza has to throw a lot due to the Raiders' defense. 

 Tight end  Brock Bowers remains a must-start option and should continue to be the focal point of the Raiders' passing attack. Ashton Jeanty has been trending down, but he still remains in play as an RB2 due to his pass game usage. I anticipate Mendoza will continue to dump the ball off at a high rate.

 As for the Raiders' secondary fantasy options -- WR  Tre Tucker and TE  Michael Mayer -- it is best to get away from them for the time being. Perhaps Mendoza can keep all these options afloat like Cousins did, but those are high expectations for a rookie. -- Florio 

 

 Did the Vikings explore other options, or was it all Cousins? 
 The Vikings did explore their options, but they had a pretty good feeling all roads would lead them to Cousins. Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones was in the mix, but sources believed he was more of a backup option to Cousins. Minnesota was linked to New York Jets quarterback Geno Smith , even if through a basic inquiry. The Jets had no interest in moving on from Smith, who was on the Vikings' radar back in March. It's possible the Vikings made other calls as they scanned the quarterback landscape, but acquiring Cousins, given his history in Minnesota and the reasonable price tag, always made the most sense. -- Fowler 

 

 How well-liked does Cousins remain in the Vikings' building after leaving three years ago? 
 

 On a personal level, Cousins was loved within the Vikings' practice building by the end of his tenure. He had a much better personal relationship with O'Connell than he did with former coach Mike Zimmer, and teammates gleefully helped create the "Kirko Chains" alter ego by egging on Cousins to take off his shirt and wear jewelry on team flights. When he returned to U.S. Bank Stadium in 2024 as a member of the Atlanta Falcons , a long line of well-wishers waited in a makeshift receiving line to embrace him after the game. On the field, the Vikings were willing to let Cousins move on in free agency because they hoped to elevate the position in a way that could help them compete better in the playoffs. What they found, however, is that the grass is not always greener on the other side. -- Seifert

title: Fantasy impacts of the NFL trade deadline: Breaking down fantasy-relevant moves
summary: NFL trade deadline day has come and gone, but we have the latest fantasy news and analysis for every key deal.
full_text:
Fantasy managers have their eyes on the prize as they hoped for new destinations for their beloved stars at the NFL trade deadline. Some players stayed put, some ended up in new cities and one ended the day back with familiar faces. What does it all mean going forward for managers and their rosters?

 The ESPN fantasy football crew has you covered, breaking down what's in store for the new additions, as well as other players who are either stepping up or sharing the limelight. We tracked the latest news through the 4 p.m. ET deadline as managers gear up for the home stretch of the season with the fantasy analysis to make the most of these trades. 

 See also: 
 Trade deadline tracker | Fantasy Buzz 

 

 Colts trading WR Josh Downs to Chiefs 
 

 Michael F. Florio: The Kansas City Chiefs have had a need for another receiver, and Downs is a reliable target for Patrick Mahomes . Downs has struggled fantasy-wise with the Indianapolis Colts this season, averaging just 8.3 fantasy PPG. He certainly gets a QB and an offensive upgrade, but he will have more target competition in Kansas City.

 Downs has split his time out wide and in the slot almost evenly this season. That versatility will help him in Kansas City, as they can use him in different formations and move him around the field. I would expect that once he is acclimated with his new offense, he plays in two-receiver sets over Xavier Worthy . He will likely serve as the third target behind Travis Kelce and Rashee Rice , but with Rice struggling as of late, Downs could earn more opportunities.

 Downs is rostered in 61% of ESPN fantasy leagues, so it is worth checking waiver wires if he is out there. While managers can (and should) add him to their roster, exercise patience and don't elevate him into starting lineups just yet. It typically takes receivers longer to learn a new team's playbook, and it's likely Downs will see limited usage this week against the Atlanta Falcons , even if it is a favorable matchup.

 Still, Mahomes is the biggest winner of this trade as he gets a much-needed receiver. He has averaged 17.7 fantasy PPG and his passing numbers continue to trend down. While this does not elevate him back to elite fantasy status, Mahomes remains a low-end QB1 with a bit more upside now.

 As for the Colts, who also traded Keenan Allen earlier today, they are left with Laquon Treadwell , Deion Burks ,  Ashton Dulin  and  Nick Westbrook-Ikhine  as the top receivers on the active roster. TE Tyler Warren is the biggest fantasy winner of the Downs trade, as he will be the unquestioned top target for Indy moving forward. Him and Jonathan Taylor are the only Colts that are fantasy relevant at the moment.

 

 Raiders trade QB Kirk Cousins to the Vikings 
 

 Florio: Cousins officially returns to the Minnesota Vikings , where he played from 2018 to 2023 and averaged 3,879 passing yards and 29 touchdowns per season.

 Cousins had been enjoying a resurgence in Vegas this season, averaging 19.1 fantasy points per game and is currently the QB5 in total points. He is second in the NFL in passing touchdowns (20) and fifth in passing yards (2,340). Perhaps there is a ramp-up period as he adjusts to a new team, but Cousins knows Kevin O'Connell's system very well and has already played with most of the Vikings' skill position players, so he should be able to settle in quickly.

 Expect Cousins to hold similar fantasy value with the Vikings as with the Raiders. He is still in the low-end QB1/high-end QB2 range, and is touchdown-reliant as he does not run. The schedule in Minnesota makes it much easier to start Cousins in favorable matchups, as the Vikings have the ninth-best remaining schedule compared to 19 th for the Raiders.

 The biggest winner of this trade is Justin Jefferson . He's averaged a career-low 56.1 receiving yards per game this season, after averaging 61.6 per game in 2025. In his four seasons with Cousins, Jefferson averaged 98 yards per game and had a 17-game pace of 1,671 yards and 8.5 touchdowns. He remains a must-start fantasy option and could once again reach elite status with Cousins, especially since the Vikings have the seventh-best remaining WR schedule.

 As for the Raiders, the No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza will take over. While Mendoza is very talented, a change to a rookie QB always adds some volatility. He is worth adding off the waiver wire for QB-needy teams, as there is still clear upside here. While managers should normally take a wait-and-see approach, there will be games where Mendoza has to throw a lot due to the Raiders' defense.

 TE Brock Bowers remains a must-start option and should continue to be the focal point of the Raiders' passing attack. Ashton Jeanty has been trending down, but he still remains in play as a RB2 due to his pass-game usage. He leads RBs in catches, receiving yards (no RB is within 75 yards) and is second in receiving touchdowns. I would anticipate Mendoza will continue to dump the ball off at a high rate.

 As for the Raiders' secondary fantasy options -- WR Tre Tucker and TE Michael Mayer -- it is best to get away from them for the time being. Perhaps Mendoza can keep all these options afloat like Cousins did, but those are high expectations for a rookie. It is best to wait it out outside of the Raiders' top two options.

 

 Colts trade WR  Keenan Allen  to the 49ers 
 

 Eric Karabell:  Allen, 34, averaged a modest 10.1 fantasy points in eight games with the beleaguered Indianapolis Colts , but now his situation has considerably improved. What's left of QB Daniel Jones wasn't throwing the football downfield often or with any success for the Colts, either by plan or ability. However, Brock Purdy is quite good at doing so for the 49ers. Purdy managed to throw for 232 yards in Sunday's win over the Las Vegas Raiders with Jordan Watkins , Brandin Cooks and Demarcus Robinson as his wide receivers. He should get Mike Evans (Achilles) and Deebo Samuel Sr . (hamstring) back in the lineup soon, but Allen is a worthy possession option for this week and beyond.

 Fantasy managers should keep expectations in check, as Allen -- rostered in 46.1% of ESPN standard leagues -- is hardly the dominant force he once was for the Los Angeles Chargers . Allen's value comes from his receptions (he's currently second among active players in receptions and fourth in receiving yards), though he can't do much with those receptions anymore. He has scored five touchdowns over his past 25 games and averaged fewer than 50 receiving yards per contest, though he has played in struggling offenses (Colts, 2025 Chargers, 2024 Bears). Purdy still wants to sling the football deep. Allen hasn't averaged more than 6.4 yards per target since 2023.

 Regardless, expect Purdy to utilize this potential Hall of Famer on shorter passes and in the middle of the field as he'll rely on Allen's ability to find open spaces. Fantasy managers should expect some increase in production. After all, Allen leaves the one of the league's lesser offenses for a good one -- and the 49ers are managed and coached competently (notably on offense). Don't assume that Allen, currently 34th in fantasy points among wide receivers, suddenly becomes a safe WR3 option, but those needing a flex choice during the next two weeks when 10 NFL teams serve their bye weeks may want to consider him.

 As for finding fantasy value on the Colts with Allen gone, don't spend too much time wondering. Jones is staying put, but the 2-7 team that has lost five consecutive games may make a quarterback change to Anthony Richardson Sr ., Riley Leonard or perhaps even the retired (they always say that, right?) Philip Rivers, if he is bored (again). Colts WRs Laquon Treadwell and Ashton Dulin don't feel like relevant pickups.

title: The Philadelphia Eagles' 2026 trade haul is likely to age well over time
summary: Whether Philadelphia wants to go after its QB of the future or build up around Jalen Hurts, it has options.
full_text:
The bright side for the Philadelphia Eagles  (2-7) is that once this no-good, snake-bitten, avert-your-eyes season is over with, they'll exit the dust storm with a sack full of valuable NFL draft capital that will make them power players over the next several offseasons.

 Eagles general manager Howie Roseman made sure of that.

 He pulled off a pair of trades -- one back in October and one before the trade deadline -- that surpassed expectation and promise to age well over time.

 The first was sending center Cam Jurgens and a 2027 seventh-round draft pick to the  Baltimore Ravens  for a 2028 second-round draft pick and a 2027 fifth-round pick.

 Then on Monday , the Eagles traded defensive tackle Jordan Davis to the Jacksonville Jaguars for a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-rounder.

 Add in the A.J. Brown deal this offseason that netted New England's first-round pick in 2028 and a fifth-round pick in 2027, and you're talking about a haul that will provide Philadelphia with a wealth of optionality.

 

 They have two first-round picks in both the '27 and '28 drafts, a pair of second-round selections in '28 and '29, and a total of 12 Day 1 or Day 2 selections spanning the next three years with the possibility of adding more via compensatory picks. It's a good time to be loaded up, as the next couple drafts are projected to be full of talent as some players who have stayed in college longer due to NIL money run out of eligibility.

 If the 2026 season ended today, Philadelphia would hold the No. 5 and No. 25 overall selections come April. Whether they want to go after their quarterback of the future or build up the offense around Jalen Hurts , they have the maneuverability they need.

 And they need a lot.

 The offensive line has really fallen off and the trenches on both sides of the ball need to be fortified -- an issue that only got more urgent with the decisions to trade both Davis and Jurgens. They badly need safety help and could use reinforcements at tight end, corner and running back, to name a few.

 This is not exactly screaming quick fix. And with the futures of both offensive coordinator Sean Mannion and defensive coordinator Vic Fangio up in the air -- not to mention the fate of coach Nick Sirianni -- there's a good chance some players on the current roster won't be scheme fits for what comes next. (To that end, the decision to part with Davis now for such a strong return may look prescient should the Eagles shift to a defensive system that doesn't value a run-stuffing nose tackle as highly.)

 With just two wins, the Eagles are in the throes of a season that feels similar to 2012 and 2020 where the bottom fell out and change and repair were needed.

 The outlook has been poor enough this season that the front office felt comfortable trading away of pair of starters in-season in Jurgens and Davis, the latter of which was a team captain.

 These are not waters the Eagles have found themselves swimming in much over the past couple decades. But in the mess lay opportunity, and Roseman has found a way to capitalize on it.

title: Jacksonville Jaguars' Foyesade Oluokun leads the way again in Africa's Week 9 NFL exploits
summary: Foyesade Oluokun - a seasoned linebacker of Nigerian heritage - had yet another superb week in Week 9, starring for the Jacksonville Jaguars as they beat the Baltimore Ravens to go 6-2 for the NFL season.
full_text:
Foyesade Oluokun - a seasoned linebacker of Nigerian heritage - had yet another superb week in Week 9, starring for the Jacksonville Jaguars as they beat the Baltimore Ravens to go 6-2 for the NFL season.

 He continues to stand out among Africa's stars in the NFL, and there were several other stars with Nigerian ties across who also had strong performances this week - particularly defensively. Additionally, Zimbabwe's Nate Landman made big plays in the LA Rams' win over the Washington Commanders.

 Africa Player of the Week: Foyesade Oluokun (Jacksonville Jaguars) 
 

 Oluokun picks up Africa Player of the Week honors for a second successive week after making seven tackles - six of them solo - and a sack in the Jaguars' 33-10 win over the Ravens.

 Oluokun sacked Joe Fagano early in the second quarter, resulting in a two-yard loss for the Ravens on third down. The Jags already led 10-3 by then, but the Ravens were looking to get a drive going to enable them to nullify that advantage, and Oluokun knocked the wind out of their sails.

 As usual, however, Oluokun's contribution throughout the win was not built on having the flashiest moments, but rather ruthless consistency and efficiency.

 The first-generation Nigerian-American has now made two sacks and two interceptions this season. He is one of only two players in the entire league to have recorded both multiple sacks and multiple interceptions - with the other being the Carolina Panthers' Devin Lloyd.

 Africa Moment of the Week: Nick Emmanwori (Seattle Seahawks) 

 Emmanwori - a safety who is reportedly the youngest of five brothers born to Nigerian parents and raised the country's flag after winning the Super Bowl last season - stopped a touchdown in the 17-3 win over the Arizona Cardinals.

 

 With just over four and a half minutes left in the fourth quarter, he forced Trey McBride to spill the ball at a crucial moment - keeping the 14-point lead intact.

 By defending Gardner Minshew's pass to McBride on fourth down, Emmanwori allowed the Seahawks to start again from their own one-yard line, and they saw out the game from there.

 That one-on-one wins Moment of the Week because it was not only a moment of instinctive brilliance from Emmanwori, but also a potentially crucial one in determining which way the game went.

 The Seahawks are now 5-4 for the season and despite not being as consistent as last season, they remain in contention.

 Honorable mentions 

 Among other stars of traceable Nigerian descent: Malik Mustapha made an impressive interception for the San Francisco 49ers in their 38-17 win over the Las Vegas Raiders, Tyler Onyedim forced a fumble for the Denver Broncos in their 26-21 win over the Carolina Panthers, and Rome Odunze scored his first touchdown of the season as the Chicago Bears beat the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 27-24.

 Emmett Johnson, who has family roots in Liberia, scored a touchdown for the Kansas City Chiefs in a 35-12 win over the New York Jets.

 There were players with African ties who made big plays in week 9 but ultimately ended up losing. For one, Austin Ajiake (ties to Nigeria) forced a fumble for the Indianapolis Colts in their 27-23 loss to the Dallas Cowboys.

 His compatriot, Josh Uche, made some big plays for the Miami Dolphins in a 19-9 loss to the Detroit Lions with a sack and a pass defended. Another, Ifeatu Melifonwu, had a pass defended and a fumble reception in the Buccaneers' loss to the Bears.

 Africa-born Player Watch 

 Nate Landman - a linebacker born in Harare, Zimbabwe - was the standout African-born player in week 9. He picked up his third forced fumble of the season and is now joint-fifth in the NFL in that department, also notching up a second pass defended for 2026.

 Landman had brilliant moments throughout the game, but was not as consistent as Oluokun. While they both ended with seven tackles, Oluokun had six solo and Landman only three.

 Most importantly for Landman, however, his Rams picked up a second successive win - beating the Washington Commanders 20-13.

title: Gibbs, Allen, JSN and more Knockout league pickups for Week 10
summary: As the number of teams shrink, the number of stars available in Knockout leagues grows. Here are the ones to get.
full_text:
Editor's note: This has been updated following the NFL trade deadline on Nov. 10. 

 The super-teams are coming.

 Ten weeks in -- and with nine teams remaining in full-season Knockout leagues -- the strategy shifts. Weekly upside is becoming increasingly important, as rosters become ever-richer in talent. Aiming only for statistical floor is no longer getting it done quite as effectively. You need those big scores in order to stay afloat now.

 

 Additionally, FAB (Free Agent Budget) funds are shrinking, perhaps dramatically in your league. Take our two in-house Knockout leagues, for example. In one league, 36% of collective FAB funds remain. In the other, it's 41%. Among those 18 managers, eight have less than 30% remaining.

 If you're in a good position in terms of FAB, we've reached the stage where you're now in command of the free-agent market. Bully your competition for top free agents, examining likely competitors for newly available superstars and strategizing your bids dependent upon their resources. Pinpoint ideal times to acquire the superstars you need, rather than tossing FAB at each and every superstar who comes available.

 That's why the FAB recommendations in this space in each coming week will be exactly that: Recommendations. If you need to open your FAB wallet wider to get the player you need, do it. If your competition won't be as aggressive in pursuit of a specific player or position, hold back.

 To the point about optimal pickup times, here are a few thoughts to consider with some of this season's most fantasy-relevant teams:

 Green Bay Packers : They roster the league's No. 3 scoring quarterback (No. 4 if going by fantasy points per game)in Jordan Love , and Nos. 3 and 5 (Nos. 7 and 8 by points per game) wide receivers in Christian Watson and Matthew Golden , but the toughest part of their entire 2026 schedule is upcoming. They've got the Minnesota Vikings -- the league's No. 2 defense (in yards allowed; they lead the league in points allowed) -- up next, then a Week 11 bye, then the Los Angeles Rams on the road. Those matchup downside points present opportunities to get Packers via their managers being knocked out, but that might also prove the trend over each of the next three weeks rather than merely exiting Week 10 alone.

 Consider that among the Packers' five opponents throughout Weeks 13-17 in Knockout leagues, all but the Buffalo Bills are below league-average in passer rating allowed, setting them up for strong finishes. Target Packers as free agents accordingly, but amplifying your FAB amounts across each of the next three weeks -- remembering that any might still only make it to free agency in your league once in that time -- is a sound strategy.

 Atlanta Falcons : Mentioned last week, they're especially relevant because of their superstar running back, Bijan Robinson . Remember, the Falcons are among the teams off during Week 11 "bye-mageddon," then they return to a miserable road matchup against the Vikings. There's an excellent chance that Knockout managers will get a crack at a Robinson bid coming off Weeks 11 or 12.

 San Francisco 49ers : The 49ers have their bye in the rearview, but they've got a pair of tough-as-nails matchups in Weeks 11-12 in the Vikings and Seattle Seahawks , the league's Nos. 2 and 1 defenses. There's also a Week 14 game against the No. 3 defense in the Rams. The 49ers' schedule after (@LAC, @KC, PHI) isn't as high-level as the aforementioned Packers', but the 49ers also have three potentially elite Knockout pieces in Christian McCaffrey , George Kittle and Brock Purdy , all of whom rank among their positions' top four in fantasy points per game. Budgeting FAB for prospective 49ers exiting Weeks 11-12 is a wise move.

 The 20 most-knocked-out players exiting Week 9 
 Note that FAB recommendations are in three tiers: "% OF FAB TO BID (ENFORCE)" is a low-end recommendation, if you don't necessarily need the player but don't want him gifted to the competition. "% OF FAB TO BID (MEDIAN)" is the recommended bid for a team with average needs at that position. "% OF FAB TO BID (AGGRESSIVE)" is advised for teams thin at that specific spot. 

 
 My favorite pickup of the week 
 Jahmyr Gibbs , RB, Detroit Lions (10.1% Knocked out, 21st overall, RB9): Just beneath the chart cut-off above, you'll find Gibbs, in one of those rare weeks where he was bumped in more than 10% of Knockout leagues. His Lions' seemingly inexplicable season lows of 19 points and 270 total yards against the Miami Dolphins resulted in a season-worst 13.4 fantasy points for the running back. This gives many the chance to pick up a superstar that we might not see again in 2026. To be clear, I am not remotely concerned about his Week 9, as Gibbs remains No. 1 among running backs in fantasy points per game (26.2) and rushing share (77%), third in snap rate (77%), fourth in target share (17%) and sixth in goal-line carries (7). Feel free to be even louder with your FAB bid than you might've been exiting his Week 6 bye. Recommended FAB bid: 28-68% of your full-season FAB budget.

 Go get 'em 
 

 Josh Allen , QB, Buffalo Bills (13.1% Knocked out, 6th overall, QB2): I'm not generally one to pay up for quarterbacks at this stage of the Knockout season, but Allen is a rare bird. Even with his four sub-20-point fantasy games in his past six, he's still the position's leader in points per game (25.1) and he has more 20- (23), 25- (13) and 30-point (10) fantasy games than any other quarterback since the beginning of 2024. Allen's remaining schedule isn't top-shelf, but it also doesn't have a singular scary matchup (with the possible exception of the Packers in Week 14, which nevertheless has the chance to be a throw-throw-throw game). Recommended FAB bid: 21-40%.

 George Pickens , WR, Dallas Cowboys (14.6% Knocked out, 3rd overall, WR2), and Jameson Williams , WR, Detroit Lions (13.8% Knocked out, 5th overall, WR3): They're No. 2 wideouts in their respective top-eight (going by passing yards per game) offenses, meaning the stats should be there at times but perhaps on more of a risk/reward scale. If wide receiver depth, rather than a stable collection of high-floor candidates, is what you need, either is worth your while. Recommended FAB bids: 12-28% for Pickens, 11-26% for Williams.

 Worthy, with worries 
 

 Zay Flowers , WR, Baltimore Ravens (12.9% Knocked out, 7th overall, WR4), and Justin Jefferson , WR, Minnesota Vikings (11.1% Knocked out, 16th overall, WR6): Flowers and Jefferson are No. 1s for their teams, but their quarterback situations have cast doubts about their ability to meet their weekly statistical ceilings moving forward. Flowers has totaled 5.6 fantasy points the past two weeks while Joe Fagnano has largely handled the quarterbacking duties, while Jefferson has averaged only 10.5 fantasy points despite nine targets (again, on average) the past three weeks. In Flowers' case, at least, the acquisition of Jacoby Brissett improves his fantasy prospects from where we were a week ago at this time, while Jefferson having his bye week in the rearview is a help. Recommended bids: 9-19% for Flowers, 11-30% for Jefferson.

 Jaxon Smith-Njigba , WR, Seattle Seahawks (17.2% Knocked out, 1st overall): OK, let's be crystal clear about his placement here, which is for two very critical reasons: Smith-Njigba's top two quarterbacks, Sam Darnold and Drew Lock , are both battling injuries ahead of Week 10 and the Seahawks are on bye in Week 11. That presents an excellent chance that the star wideout might again be high on this list in either of the next two weeks. I love the guy, but you must be prepared to navigate through those two weeks potentially without much of a contribution from him. Smith-Njigba feels like one of those players on whom to make a more conservative bid, under the assumption that you'll get another chance to acquire him before November concludes. Recommended bid: 24-58%.

title: Commanders running low on time to 'put it all together'
summary: Dan Quinn knows it's repetitive to say the Commanders are close, but now they're painted into a corner.
full_text:
LANDOVER, Md. -- Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels didn't hesitate. After yet another loss, and after falling three games under .500, Daniels -- and his teammates -- know that their season is slipping away.

 So, when asked Sunday night if he worried they had enough time to turn it around, he quickly replied, "Yeah. Next week is a must-win."

 Earlier, teammate K'Lavon Chaisson said, "Yeah, damn right" when asked a similar question.

 Unfortunately for the Commanders, it's a familiar place. But it's also indicative of their season. At 2-5-1, they're three games behind the New York Giants (5-2-1) in the NFC East.

 Mathematically the Commanders remain alive, but with nine games remaining, any realistic hope the team has for a strong finish likely begins and ends vs. the Giants on Thursday (8:15 p.m. ET, Prime Video). A win and they would be two games back with eight to play and own the tiebreaker -- if that eventually mattered.

 "We all know how badly we need this," Washington coach Dan Quinn said. "Everyone in this building understands that."

 Another loss would drop them to 7-18-1 since the start of last season and likely intensify the speculation by analysts over Quinn's future. Owner Josh Harris has not publicly commented on Quinn's job. Quinn said he regularly meets with Harris before and after games and also on Mondays.

 But in training camp, one team source said what has been repeated by others at various points: "It's a results business."

 And the results need to improve. Washington has now played five one-score games; the Commanders are 1-3-1 in those games -- and 3-7-1 since the start of 2025. In 2024, when they went 12-5, Washington was 8-4 in one-score games -- but that included a four-game winning streak at season's end.

 The Commanders were in another one Sunday before losing 20-13 to the Rams. They had the ball last, drove to the Rams' 32-yard line with eight seconds left, but two failed plays ended the threat.

 They lost 23-17 in Week 6 at San Francisco, failing in the red zone -- a touchdown was nullified by a face mask penalty -- and again on the last series when they reached the 28 with 22 seconds to play.

 "We get in those moments and we have to finish," Daniels said. "We have to make plays; that's for myself, that's for the O-line, for the running backs, receivers, the playcalls, and everything like that. We have to make plays. Regardless of what they call, we have to make plays."

 They have a first-time playcaller in David Blough, but they also commit penalties or fail to execute plays properly. Perhaps no play summed it up like the final play in overtime in the last meeting against New York. Washington drove to the Giants' 24-yard line in overtime with 50 seconds remaining.

 But the Commanders ran one play, snapping the ball at 12 seconds -- the play took too long to be relayed, from the coach to the players and then they sent subs, taking more time. Daniels failed to throw the ball away, resulting in a sack and, with no timeouts left, the end of the game.

 It has added up to Quinn repeating the same lines each week, about seeking consistency and being able to play a complete game.

 He said it again Monday.

 "What I do know is that, man, do we have to put it all together," Quinn said. "There have been halves and quarters and good plays. That's what I'm looking for most: consistent football."

 And then this: "Yes, I am tired of [saying] it and I'm not going to back off it."

 The run game, which they had hoped would become a staple, has been inconsistent. In three of the past five games, the running backs haven't surpassed 50 yards. Washington's backs rank 24th in total yards and 23rd in yards per carry. When quarterback runs are included the Commanders rank ninth in yards per carry and 11th in yards per game.

 They have shown progress: In the past 10 quarters, the defense has allowed just 33 points combined, forced five turnovers and held opponents to 34.2% conversion on third downs compared to 40% for the season.

 But that has resulted in only a 1-2 record in that stretch.

 "You see the progress," Chaisson said. "The results are obviously the main thing, but we're getting closer and closer. We're making great strides, but we just have to find a way to come out with a win."

 But that's the problem: They haven't done so and now their season teeters once again. This is nothing new for the franchise: In the last eight seasons -- only four of which have occurred with Harris as owner -- Washington has been two or more games under .500 through eight games on six occasions.

 "They know I'm agitated about it, to make sure it's the whole game," Quinn said. "Playing and being competitive is not what we stand for."

 And it has left them in a bad spot.

 "I've been in the league a long time and seen a lot of crazy scenarios," Quinn said, "so you never know how the season plays out. I'll refrain from one-game statements, but I will say we need this game."
